Enabling and Configuring DRAM ECC

See 11.12.1 [DDR RAS DRAM ECC] for details on enabling and configuring DRAM ECC.
3.7.2

Software-managed Bad Symbol ID

x8 ECC can be further augmented by a software managed algorithm to provide coverage against two symbol errors in the
same ECC word by using error information across cache lines.
Bad Symbol ID can be configured using UMC::CH::EccBadSymbol. One Bad Symbol ID register is provided per DRAM
rank. When software determines that a DRAM device is bad, it should program the bad symbol into the
UMC::CH::EccBadSymbol[BadDramSymbol] field of the appropriate register. For correctable errors, the bad symbol is
determined by using the symbol captured in MCA::UMC::MCA_SYND_UMC.
Hardware uses the information that a symbol is bad as follows:
• If an ECC word has a correctable error only in a rank and symbol identified by this register, then the error is a
correctable error.
• If an ECC word has an error in a rank identified by this register, but a different symbol, then the word is presumed
to have at least two symbol errors and the error is treated as uncorrectable.
Bad Symbol ID can be enabled using UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccBadDramSymEn] and configured using the
UMC::CH::EccBadSymbol registers. There is one register per DRAM rank. The lowest-addressed register is for DRAM
rank 0, the next lowest-addressed register is for DRAM rank 1, etc.
3.7.3

DRAM Scrubbers

Scrubbers are used to periodically read cacheline sized data locations and associated tags. There are two primary benefits
to scrubbing. First, scrubbing corrects any correctable errors which are discovered before they can possibly migrate into
uncorrectable errors. This is particularly important for soft errors, which are caused by external sources such as radiation
and which are temporary conditions which do not indicate malfunctioning hardware. Second, scrubbers help identify
marginal or failed hardware by finding and logging repeated errors at the same locations.
The scrubbers can be enabled independently or together.
3.7.3.1

Periodic Scrubber

Periodic scrubber ensures that all cachelines in DRAM memory are periodically read and, if correctable errors are
discovered, they are corrected. The periodic scrubber is configured by the following registers:
• DF::DramScrubBaseAddr
• DF::DramScrubLimitAddr
• DF::DramScrubAddrLo
• DF::DramScrubAddrHi
Periodic scrubbing must be disabled during address-based error injection.
There is one periodic scrubber per die. Unless the memory is die-interleaved or socket-interleaved, each periodic scrubber
should be configured to scrub all memory attached to a given die. When the memory is interleaved, use the periodic
scrubber on the lowest numbered die to scrub all dies in the interleave region.
The scrub rate is specified as the time between successive scrub events. A scrub event occurs when a line of
memory is checked for errors; the amount of memory that is checked varies based on the memory block (see
field descriptions).
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

383

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

The time required to fully scrub the memory of a die is determined as:
• Time = ((memory size in bytes)/64) * (DramScrubRate).
• E.g., a die with 1 GB (2^30) of system memory and DF::DramScrubLimitAddr[DramScrubRate]=5.24 ms is fully
scrubbed about once every 24.4 hours.
Periodic scrubber may cover local and/or remote dies, as it only depends on the address programmed.
There are many factors which influence scrub rates. Among these are:
• The size of memory or cache to be scrubbed (higher rate for larger size)
• Resistance to upsets (higher rates for more sensitive technologies and lower voltages)
• Geographic location and altitude (higher rate for higher flux density of cosmic radiation)
• Alpha particle contribution of packaging (higher rate for less pure packaging)
• Performance sensitivity (lower rate for more performance sensitivity)
• Risk aversion (higher rate for higher risk aversion)
AMD recommends that DF::DramScrubLimitAddr[DramScrubRate] should be set to scrub all of memory every 24 hours
(approximately), unless other guidelines are given by the DRAM vendor. Adjustments may be necessary due to special
circumstances. Refer to JEDEC standards for guidelines on adjusting for geographic location.
The periodic scrubber can be programmed to start at a specific address using DF::DramScrubAddrLo and
DF::DramScrubAddrHi. To program a start address, use the following programming sequence:
• Disable the periodic scrubber via DF::DramScrubBaseAddr
• Program DF::DramScrubAddrHi to the desired location
• Program DF::DramScrubAddrLo to the desired location
• Re-enable the periodic scrubber via DF::DramScrubBaseAddr
Changing the scrub address via any other sequence is invalid and may result in unpredictable behavior.
Changing the scrub address is not allowed on production parts. Users can perform a secure-unlock procedure with the
PSP. This requires a secure connection to KDS to obtain a secure unlock token based on the part serial number.
3.7.3.2

Redirect and Poison Scrubber

The redirect scrubber scrubs DRAM by issuing a writeback to a DRAM address accessed during normal operation. These
scrubs are used to correct single bit correctable errors in a cache line.
The redirect scrubber is enabled via DF::RedirScrubCtrl. When enabled, the redirect scrubber is invoked any time a
memory read detects a corrected ECC error. DF::RedirScrubCtrl can be used to limit the number of redirect scrubs in
flight at any one time (e.g., to limit the performance impact of redirect scrubs). AMD recommends that the number of inflight redirect scrubs be limited to at most 8.
The poison scrubber issues a writeback to a DRAM address accessed during normal operation. When an uncorrectable
error is found in DRAM, poison data is created and sent to the consumer and a deferred error is logged. The poison
scrubber is used to mark the location as poison in DRAM to avoid subsequent accesses from logging another deferred
error. AMD recommends the poison scrubber be enabled.
3.7.4

Corrected Error Counters

Registers UMC::CH::EccErrCntSel and UMC::CH::EccErrCnt provide DRAM corrected error counters. DRAM error
counters increment on detection of a corrected ECC error. One error counter per chip select is implemented. Each counter
is 16 bits. Each counter stops and latches at a count of 0xFFFF. The individual counters must be written to a non-0xFFFF
value by a handler to clear the event.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

384

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Each counter can be configured to generate an interrupt when transitioning from 0xFFFE => 0xFFFF. Each counter is
capable of generating: no interrupt, an APIC-based interrupt, or SMI. When an SMI is generated,
Core::X86::Smm::LocalSmiStatus[SmiSrcMca] is set.
In addition, two error thresholding counters are provided in the MCA bank associated with the Unified Memory
Controller (UMC). MCA::UMC::MCA_MISC0_UMC counts DRAM ECC errors while
MCA::UMC::MCA_MISC1_UMC counts all other errors in the UMC MCA bank.
3.7.5

Error Injection

Types of DRAM error injection supported:
• Explicitly addressed ("coherent") Injection. When enabled by software, corrupts a single physical address with a
known error pattern. This is done coherently (e.g., all cached copies are invalidated) so that there is no chance the
injection is lost because a more up-to-date cached copy of the address exists. This can corrupt any or all beats of a
cache line. Error injection to the CC6 save is not supported.
• Implicitly addressed ("persistent") Injection. When enabled by software, corrupts all future writes within a given
memory controller with a known error pattern until injection is disabled.
• Implicitly addressed ("one-shot") Injection. When enabled by software, corrupts the next write within a given
memory controller with a known error pattern.
When performing error injection on multi-node systems, the registers must be programmed on the die and memory
controller to which the memory is attached. Both periodic and redirect scrubbing must be disabled during the error
injection process.
Error injection can be disabled by setting UMC::CH::MiscCfg[DisErrInj]. Address-based error injection can also be
disabled by using the data fabric register security settings. Error injection is disabled on production parts. Users can
perform a secure-unlock procedure with the PSP. This requires a secure connection to KDS to obtain a secure unlock
token based on the part serial number.
When injecting errors, consider the ECC scheme being used, including symbol size. Injecting multi-symbol errors may
exceed the limits of the ECC to detect errors; see 3.7.1 [Error Correcting Codes]. A multi-symbol error is composed of
two or more single-symbol errors. If the exclusive-or of the syndromes of each single-symbol error (from the Correctable
Syndromes table for the selected ECC) results in a syndrome listed in the Correctable Syndromes table, the multi-symbol
error should not be used for error injection.
For example, when using the x8 ECC, setting UMC::CH::EccErrInj[EccInjVector]=0101h and
UMC::CH::EccErrInj[EccInjEn]==001h results in an error in symbols 0 and 1. These errors individually have syndromes
9D01h and 8901h (see Table 89 [x8 ECC Correctable Syndromes]). The exclusive-or of these two syndromes is 1400h,
which is also listed in Table 89 [x8 ECC Correctable Syndromes]. Therefore, this error pattern should not be used for error
injection.
Error injection requires ECC to be enabled. If UMC::CH::EccCtrl[WrEccEn]==1 and UMC::CH::EccCtrl[RdEccEn]==0
(e.g., to examine the injected data without ECC correction), then UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccBitInterleaving] must be 0 or
data returns in a different order than it was written.
3.7.5.1

Explicitly Addressed Error Injection

Explicitly addressed error injection allows diagnostic firmware to inject errors in to DRAM and test the ECC logic.
Explicitly addressed error injection only works on addresses mapped as "WB" memory. The injection process ensures that
the error is injected into the most recent copy of the cacheline (i.e., the injection is coherent).

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

385

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Explicitly addressed error injection is configured by the following registers:
• DF::DramScrubErrAddrLo
• DF::DramScrubErrAddrHi
• UMC::CH::EccErrInj
• UMC::CH::EccErrInjCtrl
The steps to enable explicitly addressed error injection are as follows:
• Program the desired error pattern into UMC::CH::EccErrInj for each beat of data.
• Enable address-based injection in UMC::CH::EccErrInjCtrl.
• Program DF::DramScrubErrAddrHi with the upper bits of the address to be injected.
• Program DF::DramScrubErrAddrLo with the lower bits of the address to be injected and
DF::DramScrubErrAddrLo[ErrInjEn] set to 1. The address must be 64-byte aligned.
• The error injection is complete when DF::DramScrubErrAddrLo[ErrInjDone] is set.
3.7.5.2

Persistent Error Injection

Persistent error injection allows diagnostic firmware to inject errors into future DRAM writes in a memory controller. To
enable persistent error injection:
• Program the desired error pattern into UMC::CH::EccErrInj for each beat of data.
• Enable persistent error injection using UMC::CH::EccErrInjCtrl.
3.7.5.3

One-shot Error Injection

One-shot error injection allows diagnostic firmware to inject errors into the next DRAM write in a memory controller. To
enable persistent error injection:
• Program the desired error pattern into UMC::CH::EccErrInj for each beat of data.
• Enable one-shot error injection using UMC::CH::EccErrInjCtrl.
3.7.6

Address/Command Parity Errors

On server products, the memory controller supports address/command parity to protect data sent on the DRAM
address/command bus. When enabled, the memory controller calculates parity on DRAM address and commands and
send this to DRAM. If a parity error is detected, the DRAM notifies the memory controller. When configured, the memory
controller supports retry of the affected transaction(s) up to a programmable limit in order to recover the transactions.
When an retry is successful, a corrected error is logged. If the retry limit is exceeded, a system fatal error event is created.
To enable parity when unbuffered DIMMs (UDIMMs) are installed, program UMC::CH::RecCtrl[RcvrMode[1]] and
UMC::CH::BeqCtrl0[CmdParEn] to 1. To enable parity when registered DIMMs (RDIMMs) are installed, program
UMC::CH::RecCtrl[RcvrMode[1]] to 0 and UMC::CH::BeqCtrl0[RDimmParEn] to 1.
To enable retry of parity errors, program UMC::CH::RecCtrl[RecEn[0]] to 1. The retry limit can be configured using
UMC::CH::RecCtrl[MaxParRply].
3.7.7

Write Data CRC Errors

On server products, the memory controller supports a cyclic redundancy check (CRC) to protect data written to DRAM.
When enabled, the memory controller calculates CRC on write data and send this to DRAM using two additional data
beats. If a CRC error is detected, the DRAM devices notify the memory controller. When configured, the memory
controller supports retry of the affected transaction(s) up to a programmable limit in order to recover the transactions.
When a retry is successful, a corrected error is logged. If the retry limit is exceeded, a system fatal error event is created.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

386

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

To enable write data CRC, program UMC::CH::RecCtrl[RcvrMode[2]] = 1 and UMC::CH::BeqCtrl1[WrCrcEn] = 1. To
enable retry of CRC errors, program UMC::CH::RecCtrl[RecEn[1]] = 1. The retry limit can be configured using
UMC::CH::RecCtrl[MaxCrcRply].
3.7.8

Post Package Repair

The processor supports post-package repair when using DDR4 DRAMs. This feature allows spare DRAM rows to replace
malfunctioning rows via an in-field repair mechanism. Policy decisions on repairs are the responsibility of platform
firmware. Refer to the AGESA™ specification for details on the platform firmware interface.
See 11.12.5.1 [DDR Post Package Repair (PPR)] for details on how to configure the feature.
3.8

PCI Express® RAS Features

3.8.1

PCI Express® Advanced Error Reporting (AER)

Each of the PCIe® root ports support AER functionality. This applies to both the physical root ports used to connect to
external devices, as well as the internal root ports used to connect internal controllers.
The physical root ports do not support the following optional AER features:
• Receiver Buffer Overflow
• Flow Control Protocol Error
• Surprise Down
The internal root ports do not support the following optional AER features:
• Poisoned TLP Egress Blocking
• Receiver Buffer Overflow
• Flow Control Protocol Error
• Surprise Down

PCIe® Error Actions

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

388

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Errors may be reported to an external management controller using the APML interface by setting APML_ERR_En. Upon
notification of the error, the management controller may need to warm reset the processor to successfully extract error
status. SMI, SCI or NMI interrupts may also be generated to the CPU using the IntrGenSel field.
For PCIe® AER errors, standard controls within each PCIe® root port PCIe® capability and AER capability are used to
enable interrupts to the Hypervisor or Operating System. These interrupts are generated in parallel to those enabled
through the IntrGenSel field of the PCIE*_ACTION_CONTROL registers. Coordination between multiple software
entities may be needed to avoid configuring multiple interrupts for the same event. There are separate action control
registers for errors detected by the root port itself and errors detected by external devices and reported through
ERR_FATAL/ERR_NONFATAL/ERR_CORR messages over the PCIe® link.
The PCIE*_ACTION_CONTROL registers work as follows:
PCIE*Int*_ACTION_CONTROL registers are for legacy PCIe® error reporting, which are not necessarily logged with
more detail in AER registers. When an error is logged in a legacy PCIe® error register, it directly triggers the action
specified in the PCIE*Int*_ACTION_CONTROL registers.
PCIE*Ext*_ACTION_CONTROL registers are for AER error reporting. If AER is enabled, an error first is logged in a
legacy PCIe® error registers (which will trigger the PCIE*Int*_ACTION_CONTROL registers) and then the error will be
logged by the root port, if the error is unmasked. This last part triggers the action specified in the
PCIE*Ext*_ACTION_CONTROL registers.
If AER is enabled, an error may trigger duplicate actions from both PCIE*Int*_ACTION_CONTROL and
PCIE*Ext*_ACTION_CONTROL if overlap exists. To avoid duplicate actions, the following programming is
recommended:
If (AER enabled)
Clear PCIE*Port*IntFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Set PCIE*Port*ExtCorr_ACTION_CONTROL
If (DPC enabled)
Clear PCIE*Port*ExtFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Clear PCIE*Port*ExtNonFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Set PCIE*Port*IntFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Set PCIE*Port*IntNonFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Else
Clear PCIE*Port*IntFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Clear PCIE*Port*IntNonFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Set PCIE*Port*ExtFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Set PCIE*Port*ExtNonFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Else
Clear PCIE*Port*ExtCorr_ACTION_CONTROL
Clear PCIE*Port*ExtFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Clear PCIE*Port*ExtNonFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Set PCIE*Port*IntCorr_ACTION_CONTROL
Set PCIE*Port*IntFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
Set PCIE*Port*IntNonFatal_ACTION_CONTROL
End
The PCIE<0,1><Port>PARITYERR_ACTION_CONTROL registers trigger actions when the corresponding PCIe® root
port sets its PARITY_ERROR_DETECTED status bit located in its primary side STATUS register. This status
corresponds to the transmission of poisoned TLPs onto the PCIe® link. Received poison TLPs are logged in the standard
AER poisoned TLP received register. These trigger either the fatal or correctable PCIe® internal action for the receiving
port depending on the severity level set in the standard AER error severity register.
The processor may be halted to contain potentially corrupted data by setting the LinkDis_En and SyncFlood_En fields. If
this is done, interrupt based error reporting may not be used as the processor is halted and unable to service the interrupt.
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

389

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

APML-based error reporting may still be used.
3.8.3

PCIe® Error Status

PCIe® errors are logged in standard AER status registers.
3.8.4

PCI Express® eDPC

eDPC is supported on the externally facing PCIe® root ports used to connect external PCIe® devices.
3.8.5

PCI Express® ECRC

The processor supports PCI Express® ECRC generation and checking on all PCIe® root ports. ECRC is not preserved for
peer-to-peer requests that cross through the processor. In general, ECRC generation capabilities should only be enabled in
root ports and endpoints if there is a switch between them.
Note that it is legal for the processor to send requests with ECRC to endpoints that do not support ECRC. This may occur
if a root port connects to a switch with multiple downstream ports where some ports connect to endpoint devices
supporting ECRC and others connect to endpoints that do not support ECRC. Endpoints that do not support ECRC should
ignore the ECRC information.
The processor implements a standard PCI Express ECRC control as part of AER located at offset 0x168 within each PCI
Express bridge. Please refer to the PCI Express Base Specification section 7.10.7 for more details on the registers used to
control ECRC.
The following algorithm may be used to determine when and where to enable ECRC. System bios should enable ECRC
before handing off control to the OS.
For each PCIE root port, check the device immediately behind the bridge
If this is an endpoint device, do not enable ECRC on the root port and go to the next root port
Else if this is a PCI Express bridge and there are additional PCI Express bridges located on the bus behind it, the root
port is connected to a PCI Express switch (as opposed to a different type of bridge such as a PCI Express to PCI-X
bridge).
Search all PCI Express endpoint devices below the switch (which may be below additional switches).
If any endpoint device contains an AER capability in the extended capability list (type 0x1) and sets
the ECRC Check Capable bit in Advanced Error Capabilities and Control Register (offset 0x18
bit 8 inside the device's AER capability) and the root port has ECRC_GEN_CAP=0x1
Set ECRC Check Enable in the endpoint device (offset 0x18 bit 7 inside the device's AER
capability)
Set ECRC Generation Enable in the root port (root port offset 0x168 bit 6)
If any endpoint device contains an AER capability in the extended capability list (type 0x1) and sets
the ECRC Generation Capable bit in Advanced Error Capabilities and Control Register (offset
0x18 bit 5 inside the AER cap) and the root port has ECRC_CHECK_CAP=0x1
Set ECRC Check Enable in the root port (root port offset 0x168 bit 8)
Set ECRC Generation Enable in the endpoint device (offset 0x18 bit 6 inside the device's
AER capability)
3.8.6

PCI Express® Error Injection

The PCIe® controller is capable of injecting LCRC and ECRC errors in both the transmit and receive directions of each
PCI Express port by writing to the bits in the NBIO_PCIE_ERR_CNTL register of the appropriate port.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

390

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

When injecting LCRC errors, a TLP packet must be sent across the PCI Express link in the direction of the error injection.
For example, a configuration register read of the device on the far side of the link triggers TLP packets in both directions
and cause an injected LCRC error to occur. Errors cannot be injected across disabled links.
When injecting ECRC errors, ECRC must be enabled on both sides of the PCI Express link in the direction of the error
injection. Additionally, a TLP packet must be sent across the link in the direction of the error injection. Errors cannot be
injected across disabled links.
Before initiating PCIe® error injection, LCLK Clock gating feature and ASPM within PCIe® must be disabled:
PCIEPORT::PCIE_ERR_CNTL[RX_GENERATE_ECRC_ERR] = 1
PCIEPORT::PCIE_ERR_CNTL[TX_GENERATE_ECRC_ERR] = 1
PCIEPORT::PCIE_ERR_CNTL[RX_GENERATE_LCRC_ERR] = 1
PCIEPORT::PCIE_ERR_CNTL[TX_GENERATE_LCRC_ERR] = 1

Data Poisoning

Egress Port Poisoned Data Severity

IOHC is capable of triggering RAS actions when propagating poisoned data to out one of its egress ports. IOHC egress
port numbering is described in 12.1.4.4 [Bridge Device/Function Remapping]. Poisoned data going through each port may
be classified as high or low severity (IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_SEVERITY_LO,
IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_SEVERITY_HI), or may be masked off (IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_MASK_LO,
IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_MASK_HI) to prevent triggering actions. This may be used if the system knows that a
specific PCIe® device cannot properly handle poisoned data. If data is sent out the IOHC logical port towards that device,
a sync flood may be triggered to halt the system. The separate severity levels may be used to trigger interrupt notification
on some ports and sync flood on others.
It is recommended that the processor be halted using a system fatal error event when poisoned data is sent to the FCH.
The FCH is associated with egress port 0x30.
IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_SEVERITY_HI[16] = 0x1
IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_SEVERITY_HI[17] = 0x1 (IOAPIC)
IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_SEVERITY_HI[4] = 0x1 (NBIF1)
IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_SEVERITY_HI[0] = 0x1 (NBIF0)
IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_SEVERITY_LO[2] = 1 (IOHC internal)
All other bits in IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_SEVERITY_HI and IOHC::EGRESS_POISON_SEVERITY_LO should be
programmed to 0x0.

3.9.3

Global Error Status

Error status information is distributed throughout the NBIO. Each NBIO instance however, contains a set of global status
registers (IOHC::RAS_GLOBAL_STATUS_HI, IOHC::RAS_GLOBAL_STATUS_LO) intended to help software quickly
identify whether any blocks or functions have errors that require additional processing within that NBIO instance.
Within the global status registers, most of the status bits are read-only and reflect status that is located in multiple
locations. Status must be cleared in the original location before it is reflected in the global status.
The ParityErr* status bits in the global status register are Read, Write-1-to-clear. These indicate internal parity, ECC, DDP
and UCP errors and are set based on the programmed severity of the underlying error. Software must clear these status bits
by writing them to 1 before clearing any further underlying status.
Global status registers also indicate detected PCIe® errors but depending on the configuration of the PCIe® root port,
these indications may not persist over warm reset. Therefore it is recommended that firmware and software always check
PCIe® AER registers for errors after each boot.
3.10

NBIF RAS Features

The nBIF (new PCIe® Bus Interface) is one of the sub-IPs of the NBIO. The nBIF serves to build a PCIe® system view
and data path for both AMD specific clients and general 3rd-party IP clients. See 12.6 [NBIF] for more details.
The nBIF provides the following RAS features:
• Parity and/or ECC on correctness-critical SRAM arrays, including creation of poison data where appropriate;
• Detection and propagation of SDP parity errors and system fatal error events;
• Logic to create system fatal error events, stall egress ports, and/or disable PCIe® links on uncorrected and fatal
errors, if enabled; and
• Logging and reporting for detected errors.
Most detected errors within nBIF are logged in NBIO's error logging registers. See 3.9 [NBIO RAS Features] for details.
Some detected errors within nBIF are logged in nBIF-specific registers.

nBIF Error Containment

The nBIF provides a feature to cause a system fatal error event when poison data is sent to an nBIF. Poison data can be the
result of poison data sent to nBIF, or a parity error occurring in an NBIF array or datapath. This feature is intended for use
with nBIF clients that do not properly support
A RAS_LEAF implements this functionality for each major egress port in nBIF.
The RAS_LEAF contains:
• One parity wrapper for data path parity/poison check
• One parity wrapper for SRAM parity/ecc error check, when this port has SRAM in data path
• Logic to do stall the data path and create a system fatal error event
• Registers to log the error
There are internal connections to allow one leaf to propagate its detected stall/errEvent to all other RAS_LEAFs.
All parity wrappers are connected in ID to certain parity manager, which is connected to IOHUB/RAS in groups per Table
93 [Relationship of LEAF, parity manager, and parity wrapper].

LINKDIS_STALL_DIS, 0=if a link disable event is received, cause all RAS_LEAFs to stall egress. 1=do not stall
egress when a link disable event is received.

3.11

SATA, USB, and FCH RAS Features

The SATA, USB, and FCH blocks may support features to detect, correct, and report errors. If so, the requirements for
enabling and configuring these features are documented in the SATA, USB, and FCH sections of the PPR.

4

4.1

System Management Network (SMN)

Definitions

Table 94: Definitions
Term
SCF
SMN
4.2

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Description
Scalable Control Fabric, synonymous with SMN.
System Management Network.

SMN Network Overview

System Management Network (SMN) is a packetized SOC network with a minimum 8-bit packet width in each direction
with either synchronous or source synchronous clocking. It is expected that the packetized width of SMN may be adjusted
to provide increased bandwidth over a SMN segment as appropriate to meet SOC and IP requirements. Network and IP
interface partitioning is such that the IP interface is immune to changes in packet widths or other characteristics of SMN.
SMN Network interface Units (NIU), routers and Source Routing requirements are mapped at build time.
SMN transactions may originate from the SMU (MP0/PSP, MP1) software or any IP which requires SMN initiator
behavior. SMN provides a standard interface which is the aggregation of SMN and CPL request into an IP.

5.1

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Remote System Management Unit (RSMU)

Functional Description

The Remote System Management Unit (RSMU) is a standard interface between the control fabric and each IP. RSMU
performs functions common to all IPs for security, power management and system management. Software is not expected
to directly communicate with RSMU.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

407

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

6

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

System Management Unit (SMU)

6.1

SMU Overview

The system management unit (SMU) is a subcomponent of the SOC that is responsible for a variety of system and power
management tasks during boot and runtime. The SMU uses two blocks, System Management Controller (SMU) and
Platform Security Processor (PSP), in order to assist with many of these tasks. This document refers to the AMD Secure
Processor technology as PSP. At the architectural level, the PSP is known as MP0 and the SMU is known as MP1.
6.2

Initialization

The SMU does not require software initialization. Upon successful boot-up the SMU is ready for operation.
6.3

SMU Features

This section describes SOC features controlled by the SMU.
6.3.1

Clocking

The processor contains multiple PLLs to create all necessary clock signals. The SMU controls all clock frequencies based
on current performance and power requirements. Software does not directly control clock frequencies.
6.3.2

Voltage Control

The processor contains multiple voltage domains which are controlled by the SMU based on the power management state
(P-states or C-states).
6.3.2.1

Serial VID Interface

The processor includes an interface to control external voltage regulators called the serial VID interface (SVI).
See the AMD Serial VID Interface 2.0 (SVI2) Specification for details. See 1.2 [Reference Documents].
6.3.3

Sideband Interface (SBI)

The sideband interface (SBI) is an SMBus v2.0 compatible 2-wire processor slave interface. The SBI supports
the following interface(s):
• The Remote Management Interface (SB-RMI) (see the Advanced Platform Management Link (APML)
Specification for details 1.2 [Reference Documents]).
• The Temperature Sensor Interface (SB-TSI) (see the SBI Temperature Sensor Interface (SB-TSI) for details 9 [SB
Temperature Sensor Interface (SB-TSI)].
6.4

SMU Components

Security

PSP Firmware may program the RSMU in an IP to conditionally block read or write requests that originate from SMN
masters which do not meet specific trust, initiator ID, or unit ID requirements. The two tables below describe these
definitions. If a security policy for a register exists, it is expressed through a ternary expression that describes the registers
accessibility as a function of the initiator trust level. An exception to this method of security policy expression exists for
all DBGU registers. All DBGU registers are only accessible by implicitly trusted masters (PSP). All SMN traffic
originating from IP not included in the table is considered untrusted.
If a part has been unlocked through the secure unlock process, the security policy is not applied, and the accessibility of a
register is defined by its hardware accessibility alone.

Advanced Platform Management Link (APML)

8.1

Overview

The Advanced Platform Management Link (APML) is a SMBus v2.0 compatible 2-wire processor slave interface. APML
is also referred as the sideband interface (SBI).
APML is used to communicate with the Remote Management Interface (see SBI Remote Management Interface (SBRMI) and SBI Temperature Sensor Interface (SB-TSI). For related specifications, see 1.2 [Reference Documents].
8.1.1

Definitions

Table 100: APML Definitions
Term

Master

8.2

Description
Alert response address.

The device that initiates and terminates all communication and drives the clock, SCL.
Packet error code.

Remote temperature sensor, typical examples are ADM1032, LM99, MAX6657, EMC1002.
Sideband interface.
The slave cannot initiate SMBus communication and cannot drive the clock but can drive the
data signal SDA and the alert signal ALERT_L.
Temperature sensor interface.

SBI Bus Characteristics

The SBI largely follows SMBus v2.0. This section describes the exceptions.
8.2.1

SMBus Protocol Support

The SBI follows SMBus protocol except:
• The processor does not implement SMBus master functionality.
• The SBI implements the Send Byte/Receive Byte, Read Byte/Write Byte. Block Read/Block Write and
• Block Write-Block Read Process Call SMBus protocols. The Send Byte/Receive Byte SMBus protocol is only
supported by SB-TSI.
• Packet error checking (PEC) is not supported by SB-TSI.
• Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is not implemented.
• Cumulative clock extensions are not enforced.
8.2.2

I2C Support

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

AMD Confidential - Advance Information

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

The processor supports higher I2C-defined speeds as specified in the Physical Layer Characteristics section. The
processor supports the I2C master code transmission in order to reach the high-speed bus mode. Multiple SBI commands
may be sent within a single high-speed mode session. Ten-bit addressing is not supported.
8.3

SBI Processor Information

8.3.1

SBI Processor Pins

Up to six processor pins are used for SBI support: two for data transfer, three for address determination and one for an
interrupt output. Of the three address pins, one bit is socket_id used to determine which package is addressed. These pins
do not have changeable pinstrap. The Serial Interface Clock (SIC) and Serial Interface Data (SID) pins function as the
SMBus clock and data pins respectively. The SMBus alert pin (ALERT_L) is used to signal interrupts to the SMBus
master.
8.3.1.1

Physical Layer Characteristics

The SIC and SID pins differ from the SMBus specification with regard to voltage. System board voltage translators are
necessary to convert the SIC and SID pin voltage levels to that of the SMBus specification.
SBI supports frequencies of 100 KHz, 400 KHz over SIC.
8.3.2

Processor States

SBI responds to SMBus traffic except when PWROK is de-asserted (and for a brief period after it is de-asserted). Access
to internal processor state using SB-RMI is not supported under the following conditions:
• During cold and warm resets.
• During the APIC spin loop.
8.4

SBI Protocols

8.4.1

SBI Modified Block Write-Block Read Process Call

SBI uses a modified SMBus PEC-optional Block Write-Block Read Process Call protocol. The change from the SMBus
protocol is support for an optional intermediate PEC byte and ACK after the ACK for Data Byte M. This PEC byte covers
the data starting with the Slave Address through Data Byte M and is controlled by SBRMI::Control[PECEn]. This is the
only modification to the standard SMBus PEC-optional Block Write-Block Read Process Call as defined by the SMBus
Specification. The PEC byte after Data Byte N covers all previous bytes excluding the first PEC byte. Figure below shows
the transmission protocol. Each byte in the protocol is sent with the most significant bit first (bit[7]). The master may reset
the bus by holding the clock low for 25ms as specified by the SMBus Specification.

8.4.2

SBI Remote Management Interface (SB-RMI)

SB-RMI provides an interface for an external SMBus master that can be used to perform tasks such as monitoring the
processor MCA registers, processor CPUID registers etc. SB-RMI supports signaling Alert_L when a MCE is received by
any thread or when software sets SBRMI::Status[SwAlertSts]. Each package has an independent SMBUS slave port. See
8.5.1 [SBI SMBus Address].
Each package is required to contain the same number of logical threads. The SMBUS slave port attached to each package
may access only the logical threads within the package. Core::X86::Cpuid::SizeId identifies the number of logical threads
available in a package.

8.4.2.4

SB-RMI Register Access

The SB-RMI registers can be read or written from the SMBus interface using the SMBus defined PEC-optional Read Byte
and Write Byte protocols with the SB-RMI register number in the command byte or the PEC- optional Block Read and
Block Write protocols with the first SB-RMI register number to be accessed in the command byte. Block Read/Write
protocol access for SB-RMI registers is controlled by SBRMI::Control[BlkRWEn]. The SB-RMI interface supports Block
Writes of up to 32 bytes, and Block Reads of up to 32 bytes as specified by SBRMI::ReadSize[RdSize]. Bytes are
returned in ascending register order starting with the first SB-RMI register in the command byte.

8.4.3

SBI Error Detection and Recovery

This section describes the various error detection and recovery methods that can be used on the SBI bus. The important
item in providing a high reliability SBI connection is the ability to detect when an error occurs and to gracefully recover
from that error. When the SBI connections are noisy, messages can become garbled which, in turn, may cause undefined
behavior on the SBI bus. The most common noise sources are cross-talk and clock skew. Cross-talk results when the SBI
connections are routed too close to other signal carrying lines. Clock skew is usually a result of higher than expected
capacitance, between the SBI signals (clock and / or data) and ground, which causes the master and slave devices to
disagree on when data should be stable and when it is allowed to be changing.
8.4.3.1

Error Detection

SBI provides several methods of error detection: protocol ACK/NAK, packet error correction (PEC) fields, and timeouts.
The ACK/NAK mechanism is always active in SBI, but the PEC and timeouts are optional.
8.4.3.1.1

ACK/NAK Mechanism

After each byte of an SBI message, the device receiving that byte must either acknowledge (ACK) that it received the byte
correctly, or deny (NAK) that the byte was correctly received. This is most easily seen in the case of the address bytes
which follow a START (or REPEATED START) sequence, but can be used anywhere in the message. In the case of an
address byte, if a slave device recognizes the address, it will respond with an ACK and await the rest of the message. If a
slave device does not recognize the message, it will respond with a NAK and ignore the rest of the message.
8.4.3.1.2

Packet Error Correction (PEC)

The RMI protocols allow for PEC bytes to be appended to messages. The sending side calculates the PEC, based on the
data it intends to transmit, and appends it the transmitted data. The receiving side calculates the PEC based on the data it
actually receives and compares that to the PEC it receives. If the two PECs do not match, an error has occurred and the
message should be discarded. When a device detects a PEC mismatch, it should send a NAK in response to the PEC.
No special programming is needed to enable the PEC on AMD devices. If the PEC is present on an incoming message, the
device will verify the PEC and ACK or NAK as appropriate. The PEC is always calculated on outgoing messages. It is up
to the bus master to request the PEC by sending clocks for that byte before sending either a NAK or a STOP sequence.
8.4.3.1.3

Bus Timeouts

Bus timeouts should be enabled to prevent a device waiting indefinitely on a message that may not be coming. Some
timeouts are used to prevent the SBI bus from waiting for a response from a CPU that is in a power-saving idle mode.
Other timeouts are used to allow the slave device to recognize that the bus master is attempting to reset all of the devices
on the SBI bus. Either way, when a device recognizes a timeout, it should abort its current message transfer.
8.4.3.2

Error Recovery

The simplest form of error recovery is a retry. When the bus master detects an unexpected NAK, it should abort the
current transfer and retry the message sequence. In some cases, however, a message can be so garbled that a simple retry
is insufficient. This can occur, if there are multiple devices on the bus and a garbled address byte has caused the wrong
slave device to be selected. That slave device may even continue to transmit during the retry. In those cases, it will be
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

427

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

necessary to force a reset of all devices on the SBI bus, before retrying the message transfer.
8.4.3.2.1

SBI Bus Reset

The bus master can hold the clock low for a period longer the standard timeout in order to force slave devices off the bus
(see docSMB section 3.1.1.3 of the System Management Bus (SMBus) Specification, version 2.0). All SBI slave devices
are required to reset their communications if another device holds the clock line low for longer than TTimeout, min (25
milliseconds). The devices are required to complete their reset within TTimeout, max (35 milliseconds). SBI bus masters
should use the extended timeout to force a reset of all slave devices if a simple retry does not remove an error condition.
8.5

SBI Physical Interface

8.5.1

SBI SMBus Address

The SMBus address is really 7 bits. Some vendors and the SMBus specification show the address as 8 bits: bits[7:1] as the
left-justified address, and bit[0] as the Read/Write flag, where 0 indicates a Write and 1 indicates a Read. Some vendors
use only the 7 bits to describe the address.

SB Temperature Sensor Interface (SB-TSI)

9.1

Overview

The SBI temperature sensor interface (SB-TSI) is an emulation of the software and physical interface of a typical 8-pin
remote temperature sensor (RTS), see Figure 30 [RTS Thermal Management Example]. The goal is to resemble a typical
RTS so that KBC or BMC firmware requires minimal changes for future AMD products, see Figure 31 [SB-TSI Thermal
Management Example]. SB-TSI supports the SMBus protocols that typical RTS supports.

Figure 30: RTS Thermal Management Example

Figure 31: SB-TSI Thermal Management Example
Refer to the following external sources for additional information.
• System Management Bus (SMBus) specification. See docSMB.
• I2C-bus Specification and User Manual, Revision 03. See docI2C.

SB-TSI Protocol

The SB-TSI largely follows SMBus v2.0 specification except:
• The combined-format repeated start sequence is not supported in standard-mode and fast-mode. The response of
the processor's SB-TSI to the sequence in undefined.
• Only 7-bit SMBus addresses are supported.
• SB-TSI implements the Send/Receive Byte and Read/Write Byte protocols.
• SB-TSI registers can only be written by using a write byte command.
• Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is not supported.
• Packet Error Checking (PEC) is not supported.
• The usage of unsupported protocols may lead to an undefined bus condition.
• To release the bus from an undefined condition and to reset the SB-TSI slave, the bus master must hold the clock
low for a duration of time that is longer than Ttimeout.max, as specified for SMBus. The time-out needs to be
enabled by SBTSI::TimeoutConfig[TimeoutEn] = 1.
9.2.1

SB-TSI Send/Receive Byte Protocol

A SMBus master can Read SB-TSI registers by issuing a send byte command with the address of the register to be read as
the data byte followed by a receive byte command.
9.2.1.1

SB-TSI Address Pointer

The SB-TSI controller has an internal address pointer that is updated when a register is accessed using a Read or Write
byte command or when a send byte command is received. This address pointer is used to determine the address of the
register being read when a receive byte command is processed by the controller.
9.2.2

SB-TSI Read/Write Byte Protocol

An SMBus master can Read or Write SB-TSI registers by issuing a Read or a Write byte command with the address of the
register to be read or written in the command code field.
9.2.3

Alert Behavior

The ALERT_L pin is asserted if (SBTSI::Status[TempHighAlert] || SBTSI::Status[TempLowAlert]) &&
~SBTSI::Config[AlertMask] as shown in Figure 3. The following registers also affect temperature alert behavior.
• SBTSI::Config[AraDis]: Disables ARA response.
• SBTSI::UpdateRate[UpRate]: Specifies rate at which temperature thresholds are checked.
• {SBTSI::HiTempInt[HiTempInt], SBTSI::HiTempDec[HiTempDec]}: Sets high temperature threshold.
• {SBTSI::LoTempInt[LoTempInt], SBTSI::LoTempDec[LoTempDec]}: Sets low temperature threshold.
• SBTSI::AlertThreshold[AlertThr]: Specifies number of consecutive temperature samples to assert an alert.
• SBTSI::AlertConfig[AlertCompEn]: Specifies ALERT_L pin to be in latched or comparator mode. Affects ARA.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

435

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Figure 32: Alert Assertion Diagram
9.2.4

Atomic Read Mechanism

To ensure that the two required Reads (integer and decimal) for reading the CPU temperature are always originated from
one temperature value, atomic reading procedures are required. SB-TSI offers functions to maintain atomicity between the
temperature integer and decimal bytes.
[The SB-TSI Configuration Register] SBTSI::Config[ReadOrder] specifies the order for reading integer and decimal part
of the CPU temperature value for atomic CPU temperature Reads. If SBTSI::Config[ReadOrder] is 0, then a Read of the
integer part (SBTSI::CpuTempInt) of the CPU temperature triggers a latch of the decimal part (SBTSI::CpuTempDec)
until the next Read of the integer part. This latch syncs the decimal part with the integer part. The integer part is
continuously updated.
If SBTSI::Config[ReadOrder] is 1, then the Read order to ensure atomicity is reversed, i.e., decimal part = first,
integer part = second.
If it is not possible to ensure a dedicated read order as described above, the Run/Stop bit ([The SB-TSI Configuration
Register] SBTSI::Config[RunStop]) may be used to provide atomicity of reading the CPU temperature. If this bit is 0, the
CPU temperature registers are updated continuously. If it is 1, they get frozen and always deliver their last value on Read
requests.
•

•
•

Clear SBTSI::Config[RunStop].
SB-TSI Temperature and Threshold Encodings

SB-TSI CPU temperature readings and limit registers encode the temperature in increments of 0.125 from 0 to 255.875.
The high byte represents the integer portion of the temperature from 0 to 255. One increment in the high byte is equivalent
to a step of one. The upper three bits of the low byte represent the decimal portion of the temperature. One increment of
these bits is equivalent to a step of 0.125.

SB-TSI Temperature Offset Encoding

By default, SBTSI::CpuTempInt and SBTSI::CpuTempDec provide Tctl from the processor. The temperature offset
registers allow the system to adjust the SB-TSI temperature from Tctl.
The SB-TSI temperature offset registers use a different encoding in order to provide negative temperature values.
SBTSI::CpuTempOffInt[CpuTempOffInt] and SBTSI::CpuTempOffDec[CpuTempOffDec] form an 11-bit, 2's
complement value representing the temperature offset. The high byte encodes the integer portion of the temperature and
the upper three bits of the low byte represent the fractional portion of the temperature offset. One increment of these bits is
equivalent to a step of 0.125 °C. After reset the offset is always set to 0 °C. Software needs to adjust the offset to the
appropriate level.

Data Fabric Overview

The Data Fabric is assembled using a collection of modular building block components. Components consist of masters,
slaves and transport as well as a management unit. Masters are provisioned where requests enter the Data Fabric from
other IP blocks. Slaves are egress ports from the Data Fabric, where transactions are sent to other IP for service. The

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

444

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Management Unit, known as PIE, takes care of interrupts, fabric power management and other support functions.
Transport components provide the connectivity among all of the other components.
There are two types of components, transport-layer and protocol-agents.
10.2.1

Data Fabric Transport Layer Components

Data Fabric Transport-layer components connect only to each other and Data Fabric protocol agents. Transport
components provide the connectivity among all of the other components.
10.2.1.1

Transport Command and Data Crossbar (TCDX)

The data fabric transport routes command and data packets from a source to a destination. It is built out of NxN TCDX
switches. An NxN switch allows many different topologies, such as a ring, mesh or a tree. The fabric transport is the
central piece of the data fabric which provides the scalability and the ease of assembly of the chips. TCDX connects all
DF components in the system to each other, including other TCDXs. It routes command and data packets from any source
to any destination.
10.2.2

Data Fabric Protocol Agents

DF protocol agents connect external clients to the DF transport layer. Protocol agents package client data and forward the
data to the client-designated destination. Each protocol agent is tailored for a specific type of client.
10.2.2.1

Core Coherent Master (CCM)

CPU Coherent Master (aka CCM) provides the interface for any client which caches data. It is the interface block which
connects to the CPU complex (aka CCX). It receives requests from the CCX over SDP and forwards it to the transport
over FTI. Probes received from CS are sent to CCX and probe responses received are returned back to CS.
10.2.2.2

IO Master/Slave (IOMS)

The IOMS is a combined master (IOM) and slave (IOS) component with individual Master and Slave SDP ports, but
sharing a single FTI connection to the fabric transport layer. It interfaces to IOHUB. The SDP ports:
• Master: Accesses from I/O device into system.
• Slave: Accesses from system to I/O device.
The IOM is similar to the NCM, but it possesses the ability to enforce PCIe®-style ordering. The IOS is a NonCoherent
Slave. For the IOS, please refer to 1.2.6 below, where the NCS (NonCoherent Slave) is described.
10.2.2.3

Coherent Slave (CS)

The Coherent Slave (CS) is designed to receive requests from the clients through the transport layer switches and is
responsible for maintaining ordering and coherency for those requests. The Coherent Slave design implements the cHT+
coherency protocol. It interfaces to UMC through an SDP port and uses Fabric Transport Interface (FTI) to communicate
with the transport layer. The CS interfaces with the system probe filter (SPF) to limit or eliminate probes.
CS has several functions:
• CS acts as the global ordering point and works with CCM to ensure global visibility.
• CS issues probes for coherent transactions.
• The system probe filter, when present, attaches to a single CS.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

445

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

The Coherent Slave is the Data Fabric's interface to the memory controller (UMC). System memory may be spread across
multiple coherent slaves on a single die or multiple dies. Each CS services transactions to the memory addresses located
‘behind' that CS. Each CS operates independently from other CSs.
A Coherent Slave is the system's memory ordering point for all of the memory addresses behind that CS. The order in
which requests reach the CS defines the order in which operations to a given address are serviced.
For a coherent transaction, the Coherent Slave makes the decision on which of the system caches to probe, based on a
property of the transaction, SDP_ReqDomain.

Power Management, Interrupts, Etc. (PIE)

The two main functions of the PIE block are power management and interrupts. In addition this block supports other
miscellaneous functions which falls under the "etcetera" category. Some of the functions hosted in this module include:
• Fabric power management
• Controls power zones within DF
• Coordinates clock gating
• Sequences DF clock frequency changes
• Coordinates bus lock
• Handles Interrupts: detects, distributes notifications, coordinates DF with other IP
• Register access and register security
• ECC scrubbers and RAS functions
• Interrupt controller interface
• Interrupt controllers (APIC)
• Performance monitors
• MCA
10.3

Accessing Data Fabric Configuration Registers

The DF contains an 8KB range of register addresses (2048 32-bit registers) logically organized into groups of 256
registers referred to as "function spaces", and numbered "function0" through "functionN". Within a function space,
registers are assigned at offsets from the base address. Not all offsets are used in every function space.
Registers can be accessed by CPUs through PCI space (see 10.3.1 [CPU Sourced DF Configuration Register Access]).
10.3.1

CPU Sourced DF Configuration Register Access

CPUs access DF configuration registers through PCI space. DF has registers in PCI Base Configuration Space and
Extended Configuration Space, accessed through Bus 0, device 24.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

446

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020
10.3.2

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

DF Configuration Register Broadcast and Instance Mode Access

When DF contains multiple copies of a register in the various components, they reside at the same function and offset in
the DF address space. Although the value of this register is often the same for all instances of that component, in some
cases the system configuration may require different values in different component instances. Therefore, DF provides a
mechanism to access all instances (broadcast) or single instances (single-instance) of a register. The usage of which access
method (broadcast versus single-instance) depends on the targeted register. Some registers must use single-instance
because they have unique values. Other registers may use broadcast when software knows that all components are
required to have a uniform value. Finally, some registers exist only in a single component and can use broadcast or singleinstance since there is no difference between the two accesses for this type of register. This allows many registers (power
management registers, indirect access registers, etc.) to be accessed in broadcast mode.
The following registers are known to require single-instance accesses. Broadcast accesses to these registers cause
unpredictable and difficult to diagnose behavior.
• DRAM address mapping registers
• Privileged address registers
• TCDX Routing tables
• Credit registers (e.g. to optimize credit values for a downbinned topology)
• MCA registers
• DF Performance Monitors
All single-instance accesses must be indirect. That is, the software must select an indirect-access register pair and use the
index register to select which instance of the register is being used.
Broadcast accesses may be direct or indirect.
See 10.3.3 [DF Configuration Register Direct and Indirect Access] for more information on direct and indirect access.
A broadcast mode read result is the OR of all the instances with matching function space/offset. Thus, a broadcast read
provides unreliable results unless to a register that has only one instance or has the same value in all instances. This
method is not supported for the MCA registers – a broadcast read of MCA registers does not return the OR reduction of
all instances.
10.3.3

DF Configuration Register Direct and Indirect Access

DF registers can be accessed directly or indirectly. Direct access uses the register's function and offset in the access.
Indirect access uses an index/data pair register in the DF to access the desired register.
10.3.3.1

Indirect Access Registers

Indirect access to DF configuration registers requires setup of a specific register (FICAA), and the use of associated
registers (FICADL and FICADH; FICAD for both).
There are six sets of indirect access registers, with three registers in each set: one for address and two for data (to support
64-bit accesses). DF provides six sets of FICAA/FICAD (FICAA[5:0], and paired FICADL[5:0], FICADH[5:0]) and
associates them by index. For example, a write through FICADL[2] is routed to the register specified in FICAA[2]. Using
one FICAA/FICAD to access a different instance of FICAA/FICAD has undefined results.
The sets are assigned to specific sources:
set 0: PSP
set 1: SMU
set 2: Microcode

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

447

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

set 3: BIOS, operating-system, and drivers
set 4: Reserved
Accesses using single-instance and 64-bit registers requires use of indirect access.
10.3.3.2

DF Indirect Access Procedure

Indirect access procedure is:
1. Select the appropriate FICAA/FICAD according to the source.
2. Write FICAA, specifying the following fields. Note that the fully concatenated value can be found within the
register description of the targeted register.
1. CfgRegInstID: The instance ID.
2. IndCfgAccFuncNum: DF Function number.
3. IndCfgAccRegNum : DF Offset number.
4. CfgRegInstAccEn:
1. Set to 1: Single-instance access.
2. Set to 0: broadcast
5. SixtyFourBitRegEn: set to 1 when accessing a 64-bit register.
3. For reads:
1. Read FICADL. If reading 64-bit registers, the request must be made with a 64-bit register access
4. For writes:
1. Write FICADL. If writing 64-bit registers, the request must be made with a 64-bit access
10.3.4

10.3.4.1

DF Configuration Register 64 bit Atomic Access

CPU 64-bit Access

CPUs are allowed to issue 64-bit requests directly to DF configuration register space. The address must be 8-byte aligned.
When PIE receives a 64-bit access request from CCM, it generates the beats necessary to fulfill the atomicity
requirements for the access.

10.3.7

DF Response to Access of Unimplemented Registers

DF drops all writes to unimplemented registers. Reads to unimplemented registers return all zeroes. DF does not log any
errors for accesses to unimplemented registers or functions.
10.4

Data Fabric Instance and Fabric IDs

Every data fabric component is identified by a unique instance identifier ("InstanceID") used to access component
registers. For example, to program a register in TCDX0 only, specify the instance ID for TCDX0 in the register access
(see 10.3.5 [DF Configuration Register Access Examples]).
For address mapping and packet routing, each Data Fabric protocol component is assigned a unique Data Fabric Identifier
("FabricID"). The FabricID consists of a NodeID section and a ComponentID section.. The value for a component's
FabricID is assigned at reset. Transport-layer components (TCDXs) do not have a FabricID. Address maps are populated
with the targeted component's FabricID.

FabricBlockInstanceInformation3[BlockFabricID] and FabricBlockInstanceInformation3[BlockInstanceID] self-report
each component's identifiers.

10.6.1

10.6.1.1

Reserved Address Range

Special Address Range

For system purposes, the processor and data fabric define a 12GB "special address range" at the very top of the maximum
physical address space. This address range is not accessible to I/O or CPU clients. For instance, if the processor supports a
48-bit physical address, the memory from (2*48-12GB) to (2*48-1) is not accessible. CPU page tables that reference this
address result in a page-fault (#PF) exception and I/O accesses are aborted. The BIOS must map this region as
inaccessible to the operating system.
10.6.1.2

IOMMU Reserved Region

If IOMMU is enabled, the processor must reserve the following addresses:
• 0x00FD_0000_0000->0x00FD_F8FF_FFFF (3.9GB)
• 0x00FD_F910_0000->0x00FD_F91F_FFFF (1MB)
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

450

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

• 0x00FD_FB00_0000->0x00FD_FFFF_FFFF (80MB)
MMIO addresses must not be assigned in these regions.

If the first DRAM address map (the one starting at address 0) includes these regions, the BIOS must map these regions as
inaccessible to the operating system. In addition, the firmware must use these DRAM addresses for any privileged
memory regions that would be taken out of this same address map.
If any other DRAM address map includes these regions, the firmware must boost this address map so that it starts at 1TB.
The entire region between the previous DRAM address map, and 1TB, is then marked as inaccessible to the operating
system.

each specifies a different address range. Software programs DRAM Base/Limit pairs for each component as summarized
below:

10.7

DF DRAM Address Mapping Rules for SoC

10.7.1

MMIO Address Maps

The processor routes accesses to MMIO addresses using 16 sets of MMIO address mapping registers.
In addition, the VGA-compatible MMIO address space can be mapped using DF::VGAEn. An MMIO access that does not
hit on a valid MMIO/VGA address mapping register is sent to the compatibility (subtractive) address space.
Transaction addresses in the specified base/limit range are routed to the target IOHUB specified by DstFabricID.
List of applicable registers:
• DF::MmioBaseAddress
• DF::MmioLimitAddress
• DF::MmioAddressControl
• DF::VGAEn
10.7.1.1

MMIO Mapping Rules

A MMIO access that does not hit on a valid MMIO address mapping register is sent to the compatibility (subtractive)
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

451

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

address space.
Transaction addresses are within the defined range (MMIO range) if:
• {MMIOBase[MSB:16], 0000h} <= address[MSB:0] <= {MMIOLimit[MSB:16], FFFFh}.
MMIO regions must not overlap each other.
Programming of the MMIO address maps must be consistent with the Memory-Type Range Registers (MTRRs) and the
top of memory registers. CPU accesses only hit within the MMIO address maps if the corresponding MTRR is of type IO.
The appropriate RE or WE bit(s) must be set. When initializing a base/limit pair, the BIOS must write the base and limit
registers before the control register is written. When changing a base/limit pair that is already enabled, the BIOS should
clear RE and WE before changing the address range.
Scenarios in which the address space of multiple MMIO ranges target the same target are supported.
This may be used to force writes to be non-posted for MMIO regions which map to the legacy ISA/LPC bus.
If two MMIO ranges target the same IO device and the NP bit is set differently in both ranges, unexpected transaction
ordering effects are possible. In particular, using PCI- and IO-link-defined producer-consumer semantics, if a producer
(e.g. the processor) writes data using a non-posted MMIO range followed by a flag to a posted MMIO range, then it is
possible for the device to see the flag updated before the data is updated.
10.7.2

PCI I/O Address Maps

The processor routes PCI I/O accesses using 8 sets of PCI I/O address mapping registers. In addition, the VGAcompatible PCI I/O address space can be mapped using DF::VGAEn.
A PCI I/O access that does not hit on a valid PCI IO/VGA address mapping register is sent to the compatibility
(subtractive) address space.
The Data Fabric only allows CPU clients to access PCI I/O.
List of applicable registers:
• DF::X86IOBaseAddress
• DF::X86IOLimitAddress
10.7.3

PCI Configuration Address Maps

The processor routes PCI configuration accesses using 8 sets of PCI configuration address mapping registers. The Data
Fabric requires that every PCI bus is mapped in the registers and does not support compatibility (subtractive) address
space.
List of applicable registers:
• DF::CfgAddressMap
• DF::CfgAddressCntl
• DF::CfgBus0Type1DstFabricIDReg0, DF::CfgBus0Type1DstFabricIDReg1
The first 256 bytes of every PCI configuration space function are called "Base Configuration Space" (BCS) and bytes 256
through 4095 are called "Extended Configuration Space" (ECS).
CPU software accesses PCI configuration space (including Data Fabric registers) in two ways:

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

452

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020
•
•

•

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Through IO-space:
• IO instructions to addresses CF8h and CFCh.
• Only PCI-defined segment 0 is accessible.
Through MMIO space:
• Configuration space is a region of (system) memory space.
• The base address and size of this range is specified in the MMIO Configuration Base/Limit Address
Register DF::X86IOBaseAddress.
• The size is determined by the number of configuration-space bus numbers supported by the system and by
the number of segments; each segment contains a separate set of 256 buses.
• Only one segment is supported.
• Accesses to this range are converted to configuration space accesses as follows:
• Address[31:0] = {segment [3:0], bus[7:0], device[4:0], function[2:0], offset[11:0]}.
The BIOS may use either configuration space access mechanism during boot. Before booting the OS, BIOS is
expected to disable IO access to ECS and enable MMIO access.

The Data Fabric only allows CPU clients to access PCI configuration space.
10.8

Data Fabric Security

The Data Fabric supports memory encryption and link encryption.
10.8.1

Data Fabric Register Security

The PSP controls all data fabric register security features, based on the security policy set by the PSP. This section
describes the base security policy but other security policies may be used by the PSP.

During BIOS boot, the DRAM address map registers are read-only. After BIOS boot, all data fabric registers are read-only
with the exception of the following registers:
• DF::FabricIndirectConfigAccessAddress[5:3] for indirect access usage.
• Scrub control (DF::DramScrubBaseAddr, DF::DramScrubLimitAddr, DF::DramScrubAddrLo,
DF::DramScrubAddrHi, DF::RedirScrubCtrl).
10.8.2

Data Fabric Memory Security

The data fabric hardware can be programmed by the PSP to protect memory contents.
Data fabric security features are designed to protect:
• Memory used for system purposes, such as private regions for PSP, SMU or for blocks to save and restore state
over C-states. These are referred to as "privileged memory regions".
• The ASEG regions.
• The TSEG region, as long as it is 1MB aligned.
• VMGuard memory.
The privileged memory regions are protected from inappropriate access by any unauthorized requestor. Any attempt to
access these regions from unauthorized requestors is fenced by the CS. The authorized requestors for each region are as
follows:
• PSP region: Only the originator matching the PSP FabricID/UnitID is allowed.
• SMU region: Only the originator matching the SMU FabricID/UnitID is allowed.
• CC6 region: Only CPUs are allowed.
• DF region: Only the Data Fabric PIE block is allowed.
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

453

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

In addition, the originator matching the PSP FabricID/UnitID is allowed access to all regions.
The additional data fabric ASEG and TSEG region protection, when enabled by BIOS completing a call to the PSP after
initialization, creates an additional fence to protect these regions from access from any source other than a CPU operating
in SMM. In order to utilize the TSEG protection, it is required that platform BIOS sets
Core::X86::Msr::SMMAddr[TSegBase[47:17]] bits[19:17] and Core::X86::Msr::SMMMask[TSegMask[47:17]]
bits[19:17] to 000b. The TSEG must be a multiple of 1MB and aligned to a 1MB boundary.

D18F0x0C0...D18F0x0F8 [IO Space Base Address] (DF::X86IOBaseAddress)
Reset: 0000_0000h.
IO Space Base Address Registers specify the mapping from IO addresses to the corresponding FabricID of the IOHUB
where they need to be routed. See DF::X86IOLimitAddress for Limit Address Register. These accesses are transactions
resulting from x86-defined IN and OUT instructions. IO address ranges are specified by up to 8 sets of base/limit
registers: DF::X86IOBaseAddress and DF::X86IOLimitAddress. Transaction addresses that are within the specified
base/limit range are routed to the destination port specified by DF::X86IOLimitAddress[DstFabricID]. These requests
use a fixed address for address bits [47:25] described in the Coherent HyperTransport Plus specification under System
address map. Only lower address bits [24:12] are matched through the range registers.
IO mapping rules:
IO space transaction addresses are within the defined range if {DF::X86IOBaseAddress[IOBase], 000h} <= address <=
{DF::X86IOLimitAddress[IOLimit], FFFh} and as specified by DF::X86IOBaseAddress[IE];
IO regions must not overlap.
The appropriate DF::X86IOBaseAddress[RE] or DF::X86IOBaseAddress[WE] bit(s) must be configured.

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

UMC

11.1

UMC Overview

Each processor die includes two Unified Memory Controllers (UMC).
Each UMC controls one DDR4 channel, either 64-bit or 72-bit with ECC.
The UMC interfaces to the system via the Data Fabric (DF) Coherent Slave. The UMC operates on normalized addresses
which only include address bits within a UMC's populated memory address range. The physical to normalized address
translation varies based on various Data Fabric settings. The normalized address to DRAM address protocol translation is
performed by the UMC.
The UMC supports:
• DDR4 DRAM devices.
• Additional AM4 package rules:
• DDR4 x8 and x16 devices are supported. x4 devices are not supported.
The following restrictions apply to the DRAM and/or DIMM types and configurations supported by the UMC:
• Mixing of DDR4 ECC and non-ECC DIMMs within a channel is not supported.
• Mixing of base module types within a channel is not supported.
• All UMCs are required to operate at the same MEMCLK frequency, regardless of the channel.
• Asymmetrical DRAM package types are not supported.
11.1.1

UMC Frequency Support

The tables below list the maximum DRAM speeds supported by configuration. The motherboard should comply with the
relevant AMD socket motherboard design guidelines (MBDG) to achieve the rated speeds. In cases where MBDG design
options exist, lower-quality options may compromise the maximum achievable speed; motherboard designers should
assess the tradeoffs.

• 1R: 1 package rank of SDP DRAMs
• 2R: 2 package ranks of SDP DRAMs

11.1.2

UMC Configuration Registers

Each UMC contains an 8KB range of configuration registers accessed by SMN. The UMC is logically organized into CH
and CTRL blocks. CH block contains configuration registers related to DRAM controller protocol for the channel. The
CTRL block contains configuration registers related to power management and accessory functions. The CTRL block also
contains an indirect access mechanism to the DDR phy configuration space.
11.1.2.1

DDR Phy Configuration Access

The following registers and command sequences are used to access DDR phy configuration space.
• UMC::CTRL::ApbCmd[Write,AutoInc,Address]
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

499

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020
•
•

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

UMC::CTRL::ApbDat[Data]
UMC::CTRL::ApbStatus[Done]

Reads (without auto-increment):
1. Write the register number to ApbCmd[Address] with ApbCmd[Write, AutoInc] = {0,0}.
2. Wait until ApbStatus[Done] == 1.
3. Read the register contents from ApbDat[Data].
Reads (with auto-increment): Not supported.
Writes (without auto-increment):
1. Write all 32 bits of register data to ApbDat[Data].
2. Write the register number to ApbCmd[Address] with ApbCmd[Write, AutoInc] = {1,0}.
3. If (DisFastApbAccess == 1) wait until ApbStatus[Done] == 1.
Writes (with auto-increment):
1. Write all 32 bits of register data to ApbDat[Data].
2. Write the register number to ApbCmd[Address] with ApbCmd[Write, AutoInc] = {1,1}.
3. If (DisFastApbAccess == 1) wait until ApbStatus[Done] == 1.
4. Write all 32 bits of register data to ApbDat[Data]. Repeat steps 3 and 4 as needed for each additional register
write.
5. Program ApbCmd[Write, AutoInc] = {0,0} to end the sequence.
Software should note the state of UMC::Phy::MicroContMuxSel which designates control of the phy internal
configuration register bus.
Phy configuration access write broadcast addressing:
• Address[22:20] = Fh for broadcast write to all p-state register instances.
• Valid for registers with "_p[3:0]" notation.
• Address[15:12] = Fh for broadcast write to all chiplet instances.
• Valid for registers with "chiplettype0_chiplet[11:0]" and "chiplettype1_chiplet[8:0]" notation.
• Address[11:8] = Fh for broadcast write to all registers in the chiplet.
• Valid for registers with "_u[1:0]", "_b[1:0]", and "_r[8:0]" notation.
11.1.2.2

UMC Configuration Register Security

UMC configuration space is protected by a combination of RSMU security slave and local write-protect configuration
bits.
The following describes general access privilege for untrusted agents:
• CH
• 0xD00 - 0xDFF: Read-write.
• Remaining ranges: Secured.
• CTRL
• 0x000 - 0xFFF: Secured.
The following bits disable write accesses to specified registers for all agents:
• UMC::CH::MiscCfg[DisErrInj]
• UMC::CH::MiscCfg[DisDebugBusSel]

DRAM Initialization and Resume

DRAM initialization involves several steps in order to configure and tune the DRAM controllers and DRAM for optimal
performance. Resume requires several steps to configure the UMCs to properly resume from the S3 state. The following
sequence describes the steps needed after a reset for initialization or resume:
1. Configure the DDR supply voltage regulator. See 11.3 [DDR Voltage].
2. If BIOS is booting from an unpowered state (ACPI S4, S5 or G3), then it performs the following:
1. Size available memory and determine MEMCLK frequency. Determine FCLK, DFICLK, and UCLK
frequencies. See 11.5 [SPD ROM-Based Configuration].
2. Program all configuration dependent UMC registers.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

502

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

3.
4.

5.

6.

7.

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

1. Program 11.4 [UMC Initialization].
2. Program 11.5 [SPD ROM-Based Configuration].
3. Program "Init" values in 11.14 [UMC Registers].
4. Program 11.6 [Additional UMC Configuration].
3. Initialize SDP Interface
1. Set UMC::CH::SdpCtrl[SdpInit] = 1.
• The system should not allow DRAM traffic at this time.
4. Perform DDR interface training:
1. Program UMC::CTRL::DFPM[SRSMEn,DFPMEn] ={0,1}.
2. Program all configuration dependent DDR phy registers.
1. Program UMC::CH::BeqCtrl0[DramRst] = 0.
2. Program 11.7 [Non-SPD ROM-Based Configuration].
3. Program 11.8 [DDR Phy Initialization].
3. For each Memory P-state, initiate a Memory P-state change and execute PMU-based DDR
training. DDR training leaves the DRAMs in self-refresh. See 11.8 [DDR Phy Initialization].
If BIOS is resuming the platform from S3 state, then it restores the values programmed in step 2. See also 11.8.3
[DDR Phy Registers for S3 Resume].
Initialize the UMC to DDR phy interface:
1. Set UMC::CH::BeqCtrl0[DfiInitStart] = 1.
2. Wait for UMC::CH::DebugMisc[DfiInitComplete] ==1.
3. Program UMC::CH::BeqCtrl0[DfiInitStart] = 0.
Final Memory P-state to the desired startup MEMCLK frequency.
1. Program SRSM instructions if necessary. See 11.11.1 [UMC Power Management].
2. Program Program UMC::CTRL::DFPM[SRSMEn,DFPMEn] = {1,1}.
3. Program UMC::CTRL::DFPM[S3ResumeMode] = 1.
4. Set UMC::CH::SpazCtrl[DisAutoRefresh] = 0. Set UMC::CH::DramTiming11[ZqcsInterval].
5. Initiate the Memory P-state change and wait for completion.
6. Program UMC::CTRL::DFPM[S3ResumeMode] = 0.
7. Program SRSM instructions if necessary.
Execute the following tasks if applicable:
1. Post Package Repair. See 11.12.5.1 [DDR Post Package Repair (PPR)].
2. DDR Interface Testing. See 11.12.5.2 [DDR Interface Testing].
3. ECC Memory Clear. See 11.12.1 [DDR RAS DRAM ECC].
1. Settings such as those found in UMC::CH::DataCtrl must be finalized prior to Memory Clear.
Set UMC::CH::UmcConfig[DramReady] = 1.

The DRAM subsystem is ready for use.
