DRAM Addressing

This section discusses programming of the DRAM address mappings configured in each UMC CH. See 11.14.1 [CH
Registers].
11.4.2.1

Routing DRAM Requests

Reference code is available to translate request normalized address to DRAM chip select (CS), row, bank, column. These
functions are made available to aid software development (e.g. power management, error addresses decoding, and error
injection). Please contact your AMD representative for more information.
11.4.2.2

Chip Select Decoding

For each chip select there is a BaseAddr and BaseAddrSec register. For each chip select pair there is an AddrMask and
AddrMaskSec register. For each chip select pair, an even chip select must be populated if the odd chip select is populated.
Each base address register specifies the starting normalized address of the block of memory associated with the chip
select. Each mask register specifies the additional address bits that are consumed by the block of memory associated with
the chip selects. If both chip selects of a DIMM are used, they must be the same size; in this case, a single mask register
covers the address space consumed by both chip selects.
Adjusting the BaseAddr and AddrMask registers allows memory to be interleaved across multiple chip selects. See
11.4.2.4 [Chip Select Interleaving].
BIOS is required to assign the largest DIMM chip select range to the lowest normalized address of the DRAM
controller. As addresses increase, the chip select size is required to remain constant or decrease. This is necessary to keep
chip select decoding on aligned address boundaries.
For each UMC normalized address, a Chipselect[i] is asserted if: CSEnable[i] & (NormAddr[39:9] &~AddrMask[i]
[39:9]).

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

504

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020
11.4.2.3

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Row, Bank, Column Addressing

For base DDR4 operation the UMC is configured to map normalized addresses as Chip Select (CS), Row, Bank Group
(BG), Bank Address (BA), and Column addressing.

Figure 34: DDR4 DRAM Base Address Map
11.4.2.4

Chip Select Interleaving

The chip select memory interleaving mode has the following requirements:
• The number of chip selects (CS) interleaved is a power-of-two.
• The chip selects are the same size and type.
A BIOS algorithm for programming chip select interleaving is as follows:
1. Program all BaseAddr and AddrMask registers using contiguous normalized address mapping.
2. Swap 1 bit for 2-way interleaving, 2 bits for 4-way interleaving:
1. For each chip select, swap the corresponding upper BaseAddr[39:9] bits with the lower BaseAddr[39:9]
bits.
2. For each chip select pair, swap the corresponding upper AddrMask[39:9] bits with the lower
AddrMask[39:9] bits.
Row CS Interleaving Mode:
• Swap the least significant bits of CS address for the least significant bits of Row address.
• Increment UMC::CH::AddrSel[RowLo] by the number of bits swapped.
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

505

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020
11.4.2.5

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Bank Group Swap

CPU Address Map:
• Assign the BG0 bit to the normalized bits immediately above the normalized address assigned to
UMC::CH::ColSelLo[ColBit2], such that it is assigned to normalized address bit 6. The remaining BA and BG
bits are placed starting at normalized address bit 9.
Alternate CPU Address Map:
• Assign the BG0 bit to the normalized bits immediately above the normalized address assigned to the column bits,
such that it is assigned to normalized address bit 13. Any remaining BG bits and then BA bits are placed
immediately above BG0.
11.4.2.6

Address Hash Bank

BIOS programs the function to enable bank hashing mode as follows:
CPU Address Map:
• For each enabled bank (0 .. NumBanks bits - 1):
• For each bit (0 .. 17):
• Break if bit >= (NumRowLo + NumRowHi) bits.
• If (bit % NumBanks bits == bank)
• AddrHashBank_[bank][RowXor] |= (1 << bit)
Alternate CPU Address Map:
• For each enabled bank (0 .. NumBanks bits - 1):
• For each bit (0 .. 17):
• Break if bit >= (NumRowLo + NumRowHi) bits.
• If (bit % NumBanks bits == bank)
• AddrHashBank_[bank][RowXor] |= (1 << bit)
• AddrHashBank_[2][ColXor] = 3F8h
11.4.2.7

Address Hash CS

Chip select interleaving is a prerequisite to enable address hashing for chip select. BIOS programs the function to enable
the hashing mode as follows:
1. Configure XorEn per the following table.
2. Configure NormAddrXor such that the bits corresponding to RowLo thru RowLo + NumRowLo -1 are set to
ones. For two-way interleaving, set both even and odd bits. For four-way interleaving, set the even bits in _n0 and
the odd bits in the _n1 register.
Adress hashing for chip select is not supported for 3-rank interleaving.

DRAM Data Burst Mapping

DRAM requests are mapped to data bursts on the DDR bus in the following order:
When UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccBitInterleaving] == 0, a 64B request is mapped to each of the eight sequential data beats as
QW0, QW1, ... QW7.
When UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccBitInterleaving] == 1, a 64B request is mapped similar except that even and odd bits are
interleaved on the DRAM bus as follows:
For x4 and x8 Symbols every group of 16 bytes in the cache line:
• Even bits map to QW0, QW2, QW4, and QW6 on the DDR bus
• Odd bits map to QW1, QW3, QW5, and QW7 on the DDR bus

SPD ROM-Based Configuration

The Serial Presence Detect (SPD) ROM is a non-volatile memory device on the DIMM encoded by the DIMM
manufacturer. The description of the SPD is usually provided on a data sheet for the DIMM itself along with data
describing the memory devices used. The data describes configuration and speed characteristics of the DIMM and the
DRAM components mounted on the DIMM. The associated data sheet also contains the DIMM byte values that are
encoded in the SPD on the DIMM.
BIOS reads the values encoded in the SPD ROM through a system-specific interface. BIOS acquires DIMM configuration
information, such as the amount of memory on each DIMM, from the SPD ROM on each DIMM and uses this
information to program the DRAM controller registers.
The SPD ROM provides values for several DRAM timing parameters that are required by the UMC. In general, BIOS
should use the optimal value specified by the SPD ROM.
For DDR4, these parameters are:
UMC::CH::DramTiming7[Trcpage]: SDRAM Optional Features (tMAW, MAC)
UMC::CH::DramTiming1[Tcl]: CAS latency
UMC::CH::DramTiming1[Trcdwr,Trcdrd]: RAS to CAS Delay Time
UMC::CH::DramTiming2[Trp]: Row Precharge Delay Time
UMC::CH::DramTiming1[Tras]: Active to Precharge Delay Time
UMC::CH::DramTiming2[Trc]: Active to Active/Refresh Delay Time
UMC::CH::TrfcTiming[Trfc]: Refresh Recovery Delay Time (tRFC1)
UMC::CH::TrfcTiming[Trfc2]: Refresh Recovery Delay Time (tRFC2)
UMC::CH::TrfcTiming[Trfc4]: Refresh Recovery Delay Time (tRFC4)
UMC::CH::DramTiming4[Tfaw]: Four Activate Window Time
UMC::CH::DramTiming3[TrrdS]: Activate to Activate Delay Time, different bank group (tRRD_S)
UMC::CH::DramTiming3[TrrdL]: Activate to Activate Delay Time, same bank group (tRRD_L)
UMC::CH::DramTiming8[TrdrdScL]: CAS to CAS Delay Time, same bank group
UMC::CH::DramTiming9[TwrwrScL]: CAS to CAS Delay Time, same bank group
UMC::CH::DramTiming6[Twr]: Minimum Write Recovery Time
UMC::CH::DramTiming5[TwtrS]: Minimum Write to Read Time, different bank group
UMC::CH::DramTiming5[TwtrL]: Minimum Write to Read Time, same bank group

DDR CA Phy Programming

BIOS interprets the AddrCmdSetup[5:0], CsOdtSetup[5:0], and CkeSetup[5:0] lookup table values with bit 5 indicating
coarse delay and bits [4:0] representing 1/32 of a UI delay steps. See the following figure.

Figure 35: DDR Command and Address Timing
The algorithm for programming the phy delays is as follows:
1. Calculate offsets relative to MEMCLK:
1. CalcDlyAddrCmd = (-32 * AddrCmdSetup[5]) + AddrCmdSetup[4:0]
2. CalcDlyCsOdt = (-32 * CsOdtSetup[5]) + CsOdtSetup[4:0]
3. CalcDlyCke = (-32 * CkeSetup[5]) + CkeSetup[4:0]
4. CalcDlyClk = MIN(CalcDlyAddrCmd, CalcDlyCsOdt, CalcDlyCke) < 0 ? 32 : 0
2. Adjust timings relative to MEMCLK delay:
1. CalcDlyAddrCmd += CalcDlyClk
2. CalcDlyCsOdt += CalcDlyClk
3. CalcDlyCke += CalcDlyClk
3. Program UMC::Phy::ATxDly as follows:
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

510

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

1. CLK (_chiplet[5:4])
1. ATxDly[6] = CalcDlyClk[5]
2. ATxDly[4:0] = CalcDlyClk[4:0]
2. Address (_chiplet[9:6,3:1])
1. ATxDly[6] = CalcDlyAddrCmd[5]
2. ATxDly[4:0] = CalcDlyAddrCmd[4:0]
3. CS and ODT (_chiplet[11:10])
1. ATxDly[6] = CalcDlyCsOdt[5]
2. ATxDly[4:0] = CalcDlyCsOdt[4:0]
4. CKE (_chiplet[0])
1. ATxDly[6] = CalcDlyCke[5]
2. ATxDly[4:0] = CalcDlyCke[4:0]
11.7.1.2

current memory p-state context.

11.8.1

DDR Phy PMU

The processor includes a phy micro-controller unit (PMU) used for training the DDR interface during boot.
BIOS communicates with the PMU using the following methods:
• Mailbox: BIOS waits for upstream messages from the PMU for action synchronization or for status messages.
• SRAM Message Block: BIOS may read or write the memory used by the PMU to send or receive complex
message data.

DDR Channel Disable

The following steps are performed to disable an unused UMC channel:
1. Program UMC::CH::SdpCtrl[SdpInit] = 0.
2. Program DDR phy to LP3 mode:
1. Program UMC::Phy::MicroContMuxSel = 1 to isolate the APB.
2. Initiate the phy state change. Perform one write to UMC::Phy::SequencerOverride as follows:
• [4:0] ForceSeq0BDfiFreq=1Fh
• [5] ForceSeq0BStart = 1
• [6] ForceSeq0BStop = 0
• [7] BlockSeq0BRequests = 1
• [8] BlockSeq0BAck = 1
• [9] DisableTerminateFlag = 0
• [10] SelectDFIFreqToGPRMux = 1
3. Wait 10us.
4. Program UMC::Phy::MicroContMuxSel = 0 to regain APB.
5. Program UMC::Phy::SequencerOverride as follows:
• [5] ForceSeq0BStart = 0
3. Program UMC::CTRL::ClkDivCtrl[DFICLK_SCGEn,UCLK_SCGEn,FCLK_SCGEn] = {1, 1, 1}.

This section describes the Reliability, Availability, and Serviceability (RAS) Features for DDR controlled by the UMC.

11.12.1 DDR RAS DRAM ECC
The steps to initialize DRAM ECC are as follows:
1. Program UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccSymbolSize]. AMD recommends x8 symbol.
2. Program UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccBitInterleaving] = EccSymbolSize.
3. UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccHardwareHistoryEn] = UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccBadDramSymEn] = 0.
4. UMC::CH::EccCtrl[WrEccEn] = 1.
5. Perform Memory Clear.
6. Program UMC::CH::EccCtrl[RdEccEn] = 1.
7. Program UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccHardwareHistoryEn] = UMC::CH::EccCtrl[EccBadDramSymEn] =
EccSymbolSize.
8. UMC::CH::EccErrCntSel[EccErrCntEn] = 1.
11.12.2 DDR RAS Command and Address Parity
Initialize parity as follows:
• IF (RDIMM || LRDIMM) THEN program UMC::CH::BeqCtrl0[RDimmParEn] to enable RCD parity.
• ELSIF (UDIMM) THEN program UMC::CH::BeqCtrl0[CmdParEn] to enable DRAM parity.
• See 11.12.4 [DDR RAS Recovery]
11.12.3 DDR RAS Write CRC
Write CRC may not be configured on ECC DIMMs if ECC is not enabled (UMC::CH::UmcConfig[DimmEccEn] == 1
and UMC::CH::EccCtrl[WrEccEn] == 0).
Initialize write CRC as follows:
• Program UMC::CH::BeqCtrl1[WrCrcEn] = 1.
• See 11.12.4 [DDR RAS Recovery].

11.12.5 DDR Traffic Generation
The UMC supports accessory modes during initialization while system memory requests are quiesced.
11.12.5.1

DDR Post Package Repair (PPR)

The sequence for DDR4 Post Package Repair (PPR) is as follows:
1. Configure prerequisites for DRAM PPR Mode.
a) Disable DBI and disable Write CRC.
2. Write a known data pattern to the full page of the repair target rank, bank, and row.
3. Configure DRAM MR for PPR Mode via UMC::CTRL::SftwrMraCmd.
a) Enable either Soft or Hard Post Package Repair with appropriate JEDEC MR Key and MR sequence.
4. Configure the PPR
a) Program UMC::CTRL::UmcBistCmdCntrl[CmdTestEnable] = 1.
b) Send ACT command with target rank, bank, and row address.
c) Send WR command.
1. Write data is used to select the individual DRAM in the rank for repair as follows:
a) Set DataPatGenSel = 10b. //User Configurable Data Pattern
b) Set all instances of UMC::CTRL::UserDataPattern0 = UMC::CTRL::UserDataPattern1 =
UMC::CTRL::UserDataPattern2 = UMC::CTRL::UserDataPattern3 = FFFF_FFFFh //All
Ones
c) Set PatOvrVal = 0.
d) Set DQPatOvrEn = 1 for all DQ lanes mapping to the desired repair device.
d) Send PRE command.
e) Program UMC::CTRL::UmcBistCmdCntrl[CmdTestEnable] = 0.
5. Disable Post Package Repair mode.
6. Read and validate the repair.
7. Once PPR mode is exited, to confirm if target row is repaired correctly the host can verify the repair by writing
data into the target row and reading it back.
8. Re-enable DBI and Write CRC if requested for mission-mode.
11.12.5.2

DDR Interface Testing

The UMC contains logic to support DDR interface testing. BIOS may generate patterns in addition to those normally used
for DRAM training, leveraging hardware and architectural awareness to efficiently interrogate the memory interface,
detect errors, and potentially identify failing components.
The AMD BIOS Memory Test (MBIST) provides the following routines:
• Interface Connectivity Test:
• Checks basic DDR address and data bus connectivity.
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

•

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Interface Data Bus Test:
• Exercises the DDR data bus with a rich set of data patterns and traffic scenarios.

11.12.6 DRAM Thermal Management and Bandwidth Capping
Each UMC can be configured to throttle commands based on UMC::CH::ThrottleCtrl.
• EVENT_L pin: UMC::CH::ThrottleCtrl[OdtsCmdThrotEn] if DDR4 mode.
• BIOS: UMC::CH::ThrottleCtrl[SwCmdThrotEn]
The recommended BIOS configuration for the EVENT_L pin is as follows:
• BIOS may enable command throttling on a DRAM controller if the platform supports EVENT_L.
• The recommended usage is for this pin to be connected to one or more JEDEC defined on DIMM temperature
sensors. The DIMM SPD indicates temperature sensor support.
• BIOS configures the temperature sensor(s) to assert EVENT_L pin active low when the trip point is exceeded and
deassert EVENT_L when the temperature drops below the trip point minus the sensor defined hysteresis.
• BIOS programs UMC::CH::ThrottleCtrl[OdtsCmdThrotCyc] with the throttling mode to employ when the trip
point has been exceeded. The actual throttling rate is workload dependent.
• The settings are chosen as follows based on a desired integer ThrottlePercent from 1 to 95:
• UMC::CH::ThrottleCtrl[RollWindowDepth] = 255.
• OdtsCmdThrotCyc = INT(-255 * (((ThrottlePercent + 45.0701))/145.0701) - 1))
• Refresh considerations:
• UMC::CH::ThrottleCtrl[OdtsIncRefEn]
• UMC dynamically enforces a 2x refresh rate while EVENT_L is asserted.
• UMC::CH::DramTiming12[Tref]
• Configured based on JEDEC defined temperature range options, normal (with a case temperature
of 85 °C) and extended (with a case temperature of 95 °C).
At start up, BIOS determines if the DRAMs are hot before enabling a UMC and delays for an amount of time to allow the
devices to cool under the influence of the thermal solution. This is accomplished by checking the temperature status in the
temperature sensor of each DIMM.
The relationship between the DRAM case temperature, trip point, and EVENT_L pin sampling interval is outlined as
follows:
• The trip point for each DIMM is ordinarily configured to the case temperature specification minus a guard band
temperature for the DIMM.
• The temperature guard band is vendor defined and is used to account for sensor inaccuracy, EVENT_L pin sample
interval, and platform thermal design.
• The sampling interval is vendor defined, expected to be in milliseconds range.
BIOS may enable bandwidth capping on a DRAM controller by setting UMC::CH::ThrottleCtrl[SwCmdThrotEn] = 1 and
programming UMC::CH::ThrottleCtrl[SwCmdThrotCyc] with the throttling mode to employ. The UMC employs the
larger of the two throttling modes if the EVENT_L pin is asserted when both modes are enabled. See
UMC::CH::ThrottleCtrl[OdtsCmdThrotCyc] programming.
11.13

UMC Performance Monitors

The UMC provides performance tuning resources to developers. Software uses UMC Performance Monitor counters to
count specific events that occur within the memory controller. Each UMC provides multiple 48-bit performance counters.
UMC provides one dedicated clock counter. All UMC performance monitor events can be counted on the remaining
counters.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

522

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

UMC Performance Monitors support the following features:
• 48-bit MEMCLK counter
• 48-bit programmable performance counters
11.13.1 Software considerations for UMC Performance Monitors
Since performance monitor counters are 48-bits, two 32-bit reads are required to obtain the entire value. The high bits are
latched when the low bits are read. Software should read UMC::CH::PerfMonCtrClkLo first, then read
UMC::CH::PerfMonCtrClkHi to ensure the proper value is read. Software should follow the same procedure for the
UMC::CH::PerfMonCtrLo and UMC::CH::PerfMonCtrHi instances. Software should follow the similar procedure for
writes.
The UMC performance counter registers are a shared resource and it is expected software prevents conflicting accesses
from multiple agents.
Software enables UMC performance monitoring by configuring events to monitor in UMC::CH::PerfMonCtl and then
programs UMC::CH::PerfMonCtlClk.
An example configuration case is as follows which enables UMC::PMC::CmdSlotClks, UMC::PMC::DataSlotClks, and
the global MEMCLK counter:
1. Program UMC::CH::PerfMonCtl_n1 = 0x80000013
2. Program UMC::CH::PerfMonCtl_n2 = 0x80000014
3. Program UMC::CH::PerfMonCtlClk = 0x83000000

11.14

UMC Registers

11.14.1 CH Registers
UMC0CHx00000000...UMC1CHx0000000C [DRAM CS Base Address] (UMC::CH::BaseAddr)
Reset: 0000_0000h.
The BaseAddr and AddrMask registers translate request addresses to DRAM chipselects. For each chipselect there is a
BaseAddr register. For each chipselect-pair there is a AddrMask register. For each request normalized address, a
Chipselect[i] is asserted if: CSEnable[i] & ((RequestAddr & ~AddrMask[i]) == (BaseAddr[i] & ~AddrMask[i])). For
each chipselect-pair, an even CS must be populated if the odd CS is populated.
_instUMCWPHY0_umc0_cs[3:0]_aliasSMN; UMC0CHx0000_000[C,8,4,0]; UMC0CH=0005_0000h
_instUMCWPHY0_umc1_cs[3:0]_aliasSMN; UMC1CHx0000_000[C,8,4,0]; UMC1CH=0015_0000h

Bits Description
31:1 BaseAddr: Base Address [39:9]. Reset: 0000_0000h. Init: 11.4.2 [DRAM Addressing]. Base address for
chipselect decoding.
AccessType: (InitiatorTrust > 2) ? Read-only : Read-write.
0 CSEnable. Reset: 0. Init: 11.4.2 [DRAM Addressing]. 0=Disable. 1=Enable. Enables chipselect decoding.
AccessType: (InitiatorTrust > 2) ? Read-only : Read-write.
UMC0CHx00000010...UMC1CHx0000001C [DRAM CS Base Secondary Address] (UMC::CH::BaseAddrSec)
Reset: 0000_0000h.
The BaseAddr and AddrMask registers translate request addresses to DRAM chipselects. For each chipselect there is a
BaseAddr register. For each chipselect-pair there is a AddrMask register. For each request normalized address, a
Chipselect[i] is asserted if: CSEnable[i] & ((RequestAddr & ~AddrMask[i]) == (BaseAddr[i] & ~AddrMask[i])). For
each chipselect-pair, an even CS must be populated if the odd CS is populated. A secondary decoder may only be
enabled if the associated primary decoder is also enabled. Used for non-power-of-two DRAM densities.

Trfc4]) * (2 ^ IsThermalEventEnabled) ).

10:0 RxEnDlyTg0. Read-write. Reset: 100h.
Description: Trained Receive Enable Delay (For Timing Group 0)
Trained to set the delay from the memory-read command to the signal enabling the read DQS
to generate read-data strobes. The trained read DQS enable asserts during the read DQS preamble
and deasserts at the end of the read burst.
RxEnDlyTg0[10:6] is the coarse delay, ie one unit of delay is 1 UI.
RxEnDlyTg0[4:0] is the fine delay, ie one unit of delay is one-thirtysecond of a UI = UI/32.
RxEnDlyTg0[5] is reserved.
Register Block Offset Address 0x080 controls the lower DQ nibble DqsEn. (For Timing Group 0)
Register Block Offset Address 0x180 controls the upper DQ nibble DqsEn. (For Timing Group 0)
These Registers are replicated per pstate.
.
Note: Timing Group 0 = RANK0 for all systems except 3DS/LRDIMM.

DataPortWrite=UMC::CTRL::ApbCmd[Address]

Bits Description
15:9 Reserved.
8:0 TxDqDlyTg0. Read-write. Reset: 010h.
Description: Write DQ Delay (Timing Group 0).
Trained to center the delay between the write DQ to the write DQS.
Tx DQ Delay ( 9 bits, includes 3b coarse and 6b fine delays); (For Timing Group 0)
TxDqDlyTg0[8:6] is the coarse delay, ie one unit of delay is 1 UI.
TxDqDlyTg0[4:0] is the fine (fractional UI) delay, ie one unit of delay is one-thirtysecond of a UI = UI/32.
TxDqDlyTg0[5] is reserved.
Register Block Offset Address 0x0C0 controls the lane0 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 0)
Register Block Offset Address 0x1C0 controls the lane1 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 0)
Register Block Offset Address 0x2C0 controls the lane2 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 0)
Register Block Offset Address 0x3C0 controls the lane3 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 0)
Register Block Offset Address 0x4C0 controls the lane4 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 0)
Register Block Offset Address 0x5C0 controls the lane5 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 0)
Register Block Offset Address 0x6C0 controls the lane6 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 0)
Register Block Offset Address 0x7C0 controls the lane7 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 0)
Register Block Offset Address 0x8C0 controls the laneDMDBI write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 0)
These Registers are replicated per pstate.
.
Note: Timing Group 0 = RANK0 for all systems except 3DS/LRDIMM.

Read-write. Reset: 0010h.
Write DQ Delay (Timing Group 1).

Bits Description
15:9 Reserved.
8:0 TxDqDlyTg1. Read-write. Reset: 010h.
Description: Write DQ Delay (Timing Group 1).
Trained to center the delay between the write DQ to the write DQS.
Tx DQ Delay ( 9 bits, includes 3b coarse and 6b fine delays); (For Timing Group 1)
TxDqDlyTg1[8:6] is the coarse delay, ie one unit of delay is 1 UI.
TxDqDlyTg1[4:0] is the fine (fractional UI) delay, ie one unit of delay is one-thirtysecond of a UI = UI/32.
TxDqDlyTg1[5] is reserved.
Register Block Offset Address 0x0C1 controls the lane0 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 1)
Register Block Offset Address 0x1C1 controls the lane1 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 1)
Register Block Offset Address 0x2C1 controls the lane2 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 1)
Register Block Offset Address 0x3C1 controls the lane3 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 1)
Register Block Offset Address 0x4C1 controls the lane4 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 1)
Register Block Offset Address 0x5C1 controls the lane5 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 1)

Bits Description
15:9 Reserved.
8:0 TxDqDlyTg2. Read-write. Reset: 010h.
Description: Write DQ Delay (Timing Group 2).
Trained to center the delay between the write DQ to the write DQS.
Tx DQ Delay ( 9 bits, includes 3b coarse and 6b fine delays); (For Timing Group 2)
TxDqDlyTg2[8:6] is the coarse delay, ie one unit of delay is 1 UI.
TxDqDlyTg2[4:0] is the fine (fractional UI) delay, ie one unit of delay is one-thirtysecond of a UI = UI/32.
TxDqDlyTg2[5] is reserved.
Register Block Offset Address 0x0C2 controls the lane0 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 2)
Register Block Offset Address 0x1C2 controls the lane1 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 2)
Register Block Offset Address 0x2C2 controls the lane2 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 2)
Register Block Offset Address 0x3C2 controls the lane3 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 2)
Register Block Offset Address 0x4C2 controls the lane4 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 2)
Register Block Offset Address 0x5C2 controls the lane5 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 2)
Register Block Offset Address 0x6C2 controls the lane6 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 2)
Register Block Offset Address 0x7C2 controls the lane7 write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 2)
Register Block Offset Address 0x8C2 controls the laneDMDBI write DQ timing. (For Timing Group 2)
These Registers are replicated per pstate.
.
Note: Timing Group 2 = RANK2 for all systems except 3DS/LRDIMM.

Read-write. Reset: 0010h.

Nonzero codes are the threshold value for the change in the master LCDL 1UI phase code
since the last Phy Update Request that will trigger a new Phy Update Request;
If (current_1UI_phase - last_1UI_phase) > DFIPHYUPDTHRESHOLD, then a Phy Update will be requested.
In units of native-control phase units,
Minimum value is 1. With DFIPHYUPDTHRESHOLD=1, a master LCDL dithering between two values will
not cause a Phy Update Request.
DFIPHYUPDMODE. Read-write. Reset: 0.
Description: 1'b0 [Default] deterministic timer-based Phy Update Requests; enables multi-channel/multi-phy
lockstep operation.
1'b1 Non-deterministic threshold-based Phy Update Requests; multi-channel/multi-phy operation not permitted.
DFIPHYUPDRESP. Read-write. Reset: 0h.
Description: Enforces the t_phyupd_resp time, the maximum time that is allowed to controller
to respond to the request for a PHY update. A dfi_error will be signaled
if there is no acknowledgement of the update request within nMEMCLKs_phyupd_resp.
3'b000 nMEMCLKs_phyupd_resp= 1024 MEMCLKs, default value
3'b001 nMEMCLKs_phyupd_resp= 2048 MEMCLKs
3'b010 nMEMCLKs_phyupd_resp= 4096 MEMCLKs
3'b011 nMEMCLKs_phyupd_resp= 8192 MEMCLKs, [not allowed in LPDDR3, LPDDR4 modes]
Any code not enumerated above is RSVD and should not be set.
DFIPHYUPDCNT. Read-write. Reset: 7h.
Description: This controls the interval between the end of a phyupdate transaction and a subsequent request.
4'b0000 - Disable timer-based Phy Update when DFIPHYUPDMODE==1'b0
4'b0001 - 16K MEMCLKs minus nMEMCLKs_phyupd_resp
4'b0011 - 32K MEMCLKs minus nMEMCLKs_phyupd_resp
4'b0111 - 64K MEMCLKs minus nMEMCLKs_phyupd_resp
4'b1111 - 128K MEMCLKs minus nMEMCLKs_phyupd_resp
Any code not enumerated above is RSVD and should not be set.

5 CalOnce. Read-write. Reset: 0.
Description: The setting of this CSR changes the behaviour of CSR CalRun.
1: The 0->1 transition of CSR CalRun causes a single iteration of the calibration
sequence to occur. Once the calibration is complete, the calibration engine
will remain IDLE until another CalRun Trigger.
0: Calibration will proceed at the rate determined by Register CalInterval.
This field should only be changed while the calibrator is idle.
ie before csr CalRun is set.
4 CalRun. Read-write. Reset: 0.
Description: 1: A calibration sequence will be triggered by the 0->1 transition of this
bit, as determined by CSR CalOnce.
0: Calibrator will not run. If already active then it will complete the current
sequence before quiescing.
The default value of this field is 0 because the calibrator needs to know whether
it is in D3 mode before it starts up.
This csr won't do anything while CalZap is asserted.

0 : 0 (continuous)
1 : 0.013
2 : 0.10
3:1
4:2
5:3
6:4
7:8
8 : 10

Description: PHY VT Drift Alarm interrupt. Assertion of this interrupt indicates the number of tap
points in the master DLL has shifted by an amount greater than 2 * DfiPhyUpdIntThreshold.
There is one bit for each master DLL and they are fully independent of one another.

PHY Initialization Engine has been fully loaded and the PHY is ready and able to assert
dfi_init_complete following the assertion of dfi_init_start. It is possible this
interrupt may not assert until after dfi_init_complete has asserted, depending on when

12.1

IOHC

12.1.1

Definitions

Table 136: Link Definitions

IOHUB Core. The I/O crossbar.

12.1.2

Architecture

The IOHC is the I/O crossbar which sits below the Data Fabric. It is responsible for routing requests between the Data
Fabric, IOMMU, IOAPIC, FCH/SCH, and multiple PCI Express root ports.
12.1.3

Register Access

The majority of IOHC registers are only indirectly accessible from CPU software. Software may use any of the
SMN_INDEX/SMN_DATA pairs or may use the SMN MMIO aperture on the same node as the target IOHC.
12.1.3.1

SMN_INDEX/SMN_DATA

The IOHC provides multiple SMN_INDEX/SMN_DATA pairs within configuration space to provide generic access to
SMN registers on the same node. There are 4 index/data pairs located in the NBCONFIG configuration space (IOHC
primary bus number, device 0, function 0) for software to use. Each PCI Express root port configuration space also
contains an index/data pair.
The target SMN address is programmed into SMN_INDEX and the target register is accessed using SMN_DATA.
This is the assigned mapping of SMN_INDEX/SMN_DATA pairs to software agents:
IOHC::NB_SMN_INDEX_0 / IOHC::NB_SMN_DATA_0: Software application
IOHC::NB_SMN_INDEX_1 / IOHC::NB_SMN_DATA_1: Reserved for OEM
IOHC::NB_SMN_INDEX_2 / IOHC::NB_SMN_DATA_2: BIOS (existing usage)
12.1.4

Initialization

Many of the IOHC registers needed to control address decoding and transaction routing are standard PCI-PCI bridge
registers associated with each of the PCI Express root ports. Standard PCI enumeration routines may be used to initialize
these registers. The following sections describe additional proprietary registers which must be programmed prior to PCI
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

700

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

enumeration.
12.1.4.1

General Settings

SBIOS must set the following registers for proper operation.
12.1.4.2

Configuring Non-PCI Resources

IOHC supports several MMIO resources which are configured outside of the standard PCI enumeration process. SBIOS
must reserve these resources and prevent them from being assigned again during PCI enumeration. Non-PCI MMIO
resources within a node must be grouped together and placed adjacent to one of the PCI MMIO ranges assigned to the
node. The concatenated range may then be covered by a single Data Fabric MMIO address map entry. In an 8-node
system, each instance of IOHC may only be allocated one 32-bit MMIO range and one 48-bit MMIO range within the
Data Fabric MMIO address map.
Each base address register contains an enable bit and a lock bit . The lock bit prevents further modifications to the enable
and address controls for that resource. Software must set the lock bits after enabling each resource. The IOMMU resource
does not have a lock bit but is automatically locked once the address range is enabled.

PCI Express® Configuration Cycle Hardware Retry on CRS

When issuing configuration cycles on the PCI Express bus, the target may respond with Configuration Request Retry
Status (CRS). This typically happens immediately after the link is initialized, or after a reset event such as a hot reset or
function-level reset. The following registers should be configured to enable hardware to automatically retry the request. If
the target does not respond within the programmed limit, the request is terminated with a master abort and all-F data.
Note: A PCI Express compliant device must become Configuration-Ready within 1s.

Software may subsequently enable CRS software visibility. This automatically disables the hardware retry feature for

12.1.4.4

Bridge Device/Function Remapping

The device and function numbers of the PCI Express root complex bridges may be reprogrammed during initialization.
This can be done to impact the order of PCI enumeration and resource assignment. Software may only swap device and
function numbers between bridges. Bridges should not be allocated a device and function number pair which is not
allocated to a bridge at reset.
Within the IOHC and IOAPIC some bridge features are programmed based on the logical bridge number and some are
programmed based on the physical bridge number. The logical bridge number is based on the software assigned device
and function number for a bridge. The physical bridge number is based on the default device and function number of the
bridge.

12.1.4.5

PCI Express® Vendor Defined Message Support (VDM)

In order to properly support ID-routed VDMs, each instance of IOHC must be programmed with the PCI bus number
ranges associated with each node in the system. Each IOHC contains several copies of the
IOHC::PCIE_VDM_NODE_CTRL4_n[*:0] register with each copy used to describe the PCI bus range owned by a node.
The associated node present bits must be set for each valid bus range.
If IOHC::PCIE_VDM_CNTL2[VdmP2pMode] == 1, then each instance of IOHC must have the node present bit cleared
for its own bus range.

Legacy PM_PME and HotPlugGPE Message to SCH

Legacy PM_PME and HotPlugGPE messages may be sent from the PCIe® root complex bridges to the Server Controller
Hub (SCH) to trigger an Server Controller Interrupt (SCI).
12.1.4.7

PME_Turn_Off

Software may send a broadcast PME_Turn_Off message out all PCIe® root ports on a node using the following sequence:
1. IOHC::NB_PCI_ARB[PMETarget] = 0
2. IOHC::NB_PCI_ARB[PMETurnOff] = 0
3. IOHC::NB_PCI_ARB[PMETurnOff] = 1
Software may send a directed PME_Turn_Off message out a specific PCIe® root ports on a node using the following
sequence:
1. IOHC::NB_PCI_ARB[PMETarget] = Logical Bridge {Device, Function} Number
2. IOHC::NB_PCI_ARB[PMETurnOff] = 0
3. IOHC::NB_PCI_ARB[PMETurnOff] = 1
12.1.5

Peer-to-Peer Support

The processor supports passing high bandwidth peer-to-peer memory read and write operations between I/O devices. Any
PCIe® device may be a source or target of a P2P operation. Additionally, internal peripherals such as the CCP or NTB
may also be the source or target of a P2P operation.
To generate a peer-to-peer request, an I/O device generates a DMA read or write operation containing an MMIO address
rather than a DRAM address.
12.1.5.1

Peer-to-Peer Synchronization

In order to optimize DMA performance to DRAM, the processor limits the methods peer I/O devices may use to
synchronize between each other in order to achieve producer/consumer ordering. These methods are a subset of what is
allowed for in the PCIe® specification.
12.1.5.1.1

Peer-to-Peer Status Polling

After issuing a set of P2P write operations, a P2P source may ensure that they are flushed to the target by performing a
subsequent P2P read operation to the same target. The P2P source may then signal that the peer writes have been
completed by setting an internal status register that is polled by the P2P target.
If the P2P source does not have read permissions to access the target, as enforced by the IOMMU, a zero-byte read
operation may still be used.
12.1.5.1.2

Writing Data and Flag to a Peer

After issuing a set of P2P write operations, a P2P source may signal the target that the writes have completed by writing a
status flag to the target also using a P2P write with RO=0. The target may either locally poll the status flag or the P2P
write may trigger hardware that then operates on the received P2P write data.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

705

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020
12.1.5.1.3

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Signaling via the CPU

After issuing a set of P2P write operations, a P2P source may signal the target indirectly via the CPU. It may generate an
interrupt or write a flag into DRAM that is polled by the CPU. The CPU would then do an MMIO write to the P2P target
to indicate that the P2P writes have been delivered from the P2P source.
12.1.5.1.4

Unsupported Peer-to-Peer Synchronization Methods

The processor does not support the below peer-to-peer synchronization methods.
Case 1:
Any synchronization scheme that relies on completions pushing posted writes in the downstream direction away from the
processor is not supported.
In the following example, the read response of the status register in step 3 may pass the P2P writes in step 1.
1. Device A does P2P writes to device B.
2. Device A sets an internal status register to indicate the P2P writes are complete.
3. In parallel, device B polls the status register in device A.
In order to make the case pass, device A may use a flushing read to device B before setting the internal status register in
step 2.
Case 2:
Any synchronization scheme that relies on ordering between the writes of one device and the reads and writes of another
device is not supported, regardless of whether or not the operations target DRAM or a 3rd I/O device.
In the following example, it is possible that the DMA operations from device B in step 3 may pass the DMA writes in step
1.
1. Device A does DMA writes to DRAM.
2. Device A does a P2P write to device B to indicate that data has been written to DRAM.
3. Once device B observes the write in step 2, device B does DMA reads or writes to the same DRAM locations
accessed by device A and requires that these operations will be ordered after the writes in step 1.
In order to make this case pass, device A should perform a flushing read to DRAM before issuing the P2P write to device
B in step 2.
Similarly, for the following example it is possible that the P2P operations in step 3 may reach device C before the P2P
writes in step 1.
1. Device A does P2P writes to device C.
2. Device A does a P2P write to device B to indicate that data has been written to device C.
3. Once device B observes the write in step 2, device B does P2P reads or writes to device C to operate on the data
sent by device A or otherwise assumes that these operations will be ordered after the writes in step 1.
In order to make this case pass, device A should perform a flushing read to device C before issuing the P2P write to device
B in step 2.
12.1.5.2

Peer-to-Peer Interaction with PCIe® ACS

The processor PCIe® root ports treat a received completion that does not match a corresponding non-posted request
previously issued by the same root port as an unexpected completion. Configurations that generate non-matching
completions to the root ports are not supported. Non-matching completions may be sent to a root port during specific
combinations of peer-to-peer traffic in conjunction with an external PCIe® switch and specific settings of the PCIe® ACS

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

706

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

features in the switch. In these cases, completions to peer-to-peer requests do not follow the reverse of the request path
back to the requester through the PCIe® topology.
In general, if IOMMU is enabled, software should enable ACS Request Redirection, ACS Upstream Forwarding, and ACS
Completion Redirection in root ports, external switches and multi-function endpoints to ensure that DMA requests are
forced up towards the IOMMU for translation. ACS Direct Translated P2P should be disabled in switches to avoid
triggering unexpected completions at the processor root ports unless one of the enabling conditions described below is
met.
At least one of the following sets of requirements must be met before ACS Direct Translated P2P may be enabled in an
external PCIe® switch downstream port or in a multi-function endpoint:
• All of the following are true:
1. At least one of the functions located behind the switch downstream port or in the multi-function endpoint
generates translated peer-to-peer requests.
2. None of the endpoints located behind the switch downstream port or in the multi-function endpoint
generate translated peer-to-peer reads or atomics.
• Or all of the following are true:
1. At least one of the functions below the switch downstream port or in the multi-function endpoint is
capable of generating translated peer-to-peer requests.
2. The peer-to-peer traffic in (1) is capable of targeting one or more functions behind one of the downstream
ports of the same switch or in the same multi-function endpoint.
3. All of the targets in (2) are not also targets of untranslated peer-to-peer traffic whose source is located
behind one of downstream ports of the same switch or in the same multi-function endpoint. PCIe®
completion redirection must be disabled in the switch downstream ports or the multi-function endpoint in
(3).
Similarly, the processor root ports will trigger a timeout event if the root port issues downstream non-posted request
without the corresponding completion returning to the same root port. This can occur whenever PCIe® ACS features are
enabled such that a function located behind a switch generates a P2P read or atomic targeting an endpoint located behind
the same switch, where the request is routed through the PCIe® root port, but the completion is directly routed back to the
originator without going back through the PCIe® root port.

Lower 32-bit field of TimeSlot
_nbio0_n[4:0]_aliasSMN; IOAGR3x0000_[14,10,0C,08,04]08; IOAGR3=15E0_0000h

Bits Description
31:0 IOAGR_SION_S0_Client_Req_TimeSlot_Lower. Read-write. Reset: 0000_0000h.
Description: Lower 32-bit field of TimeSlot[63:0]. Every 4-bits sets the arbitration decision for a new timeslot,
for a total of 16 timeslots, per given source client.
Bits 3:0 are for timeslot 0, Bits 7:4 are for timeslot 1, Bits 11:8 are for timeslot 2, etc.
A value of 0 means round-robin, value 1 means choose VC0, value 2 means choose VC1, value 3 means choose
VC2, etc. If the winner is not available, round-robin is used to pick a new winner.

VC2, etc. If the winner is not available, round-robin is used to pick a new winner.

Bits Description
31:0 RdRsp_TimeSlot_Lower. Read-write. Reset: 0000_0000h.
Description: Lower 32-bit field of TimeSlot[63:0]. Every 4-bits sets the arbitration decision for a new timeslot,

A value of 0 means round-robin, value 1 means choose Source0, value 2 means choose Source1, value 3 means
choose Source2, etc. If the winner is not available, round-robin is used to pick a new winner.

12.2

IOAPIC

12.2.1

Overview

Each instance of IOHub in the system contains an IOAPIC, separate from the IOAPIC in the FCH. When the system is in
APIC mode, the IOHub IOAPIC services legacy INTx interrupts from the PCIe® root complex ports on the same node.
When the system is in PIC mode, legacy INTx interrupts flow through the mapping logic at the front end of the IOHub
IOAPIC and are then redirected to the PIC in the FCH.
12.2.2

Register Access

The IOHub IOAPIC features a standard set of IOAPIC MMIO registers. The MMIO aperture is controlled by the IOHC.
Proprietary control registers are accessed through the various SMN access methods such as SMN_INDEX/SMN_DATA.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

880

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020
12.2.3

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Initialization

Many of the IOHC registers needed to control address decoding and transaction routing are standard PCI-PCI bridge
registers associated with each of the PCI Express root ports. Standard PCI enumeration routines may be used to initialize
these registers. The following sections describe additional proprietary registers which must be programmed prior to PCI
enumeration.
12.2.3.1

IOAPIC Initialization

The configuration of the IOAPIC MMIO base address is described in 12.1.4.2 [Configuring Non-PCI Resources].
The IOAPIC has up to a total of 90 interrupt inputs grouped as 5 interrupts per PCIe® root complex bridge. Each root
complex bridge supports 4 interrupts corresponding to INT A/B/C/D from the PCIe® link and an additional interrupt from
the bridge itself to support features like PME and AER.
Interrupt inputs are swizzled and mapped onto one of 32 IOAPIC redirection table entries. The recommended interrupt
routing and swizzling configuration is shown in the table below for each logical bridge. Additional information about
logical bridge numbering and its association with the root port bus/device/function number is covered in 12.1.4.4 [Bridge
Device/Function Remapping].

PIC Mode

When the system is in PIC mode, INTx interrupts are still mapped onto the 32 redirection table entries of the IOAPIC.
These are then reduced modulo 8 onto 8 interrupts (INT A-H) that are forwarded to the PIC in the FCH.
In a multi-node system the INT A-H interrupts are sent from each node and are logically ORed together before being sent
to FCH. No swizzling is performed between the IOAPIC and the PIC.

12.3

IOMMU

The I/O Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) extends the AMD64 system architecture by adding support for address
translation and system memory access protection on DMA transfers from peripheral devices.
12.3.1

Functional Description

12.3.1.1

Definitions

Table 142: Link Definitions
Term
Description
IOMMU
IO Memory Management Unit
12.3.1.2

Programming Reference

12.3.1.2.1

IOMMU SMI Filtering

To ensure system management interrupts come from valid peripheral sources, the IOMMU supports an SMI filter
(IOMMUMMIO::IOMMU_MMIO_EFR_0[SMIF_SUP] == 01b). SMI interrupts are filtered according to the values
programmed in the SMI filter registers. The registers specify what sources are allowed to send SMI interrupts.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

889

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

IOMMUMMIO::IOMMU_MMIO_EFR_0[SMIF_RC] indicates the number of SMI filter registers available.
The BIOS should set up the SMI filter registers and lock them. These settings take effect when system software enables
the IOMMU and enables SMI filtering. BIOS should perform the following steps to set up SMI filtering:
1. Choose an SMI filter register from the available set described in
IOMMUMMIO::IOMMU_MMIO_EFR_0[SMIF_RC]. Select one register for each SMI source.
2. Program selected SMI filter register to the Device ID of the peripheral issuing the SMI interrupts via
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_0_0[SmiDID_0],
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_1_0[SmiDID_1],
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_2_0[SmiDID_2],
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_3_0[SmiDID_3]. Program one register for each SMI source.
3. Program selected SMI filter register to be valid via IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_0_0[SmiDV_0],
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_1_0[SmiDV_1],
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_2_0[SmiDV_2],
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_3_0[SmiDV_3]. Program one register for each SMI source.
4. Program selected SMI filter register to be locked via
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_0_0[SmiFLock_0],
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_1_0[SmiFLock_1],
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_2_0[SmiFLock_2],
IOMMUMMIO::SMI_FILTER_REGISTER_3_0[SmiFLock_3]. Program one register for each SMI source.

Bank-Lock Register [MMIO Offset 4018h]. Each supported event counter bank is in a distinct, consecutive 4K
byte page. The limit of 63 counter banks is architectural and an implementation may set a lower value.
0=No event counter banks supported.
1-63=The number of event counter banks supported.
Note: IOMMU event counter banks are numbered starting with 0.

10:7 N_COUNTER. Read-only. Reset: Fixed,4h.
Description: Reports the number of individual counters in each IOMMU counter bank. Each counter bank
contains the same number of counters.
0=No counters supported.
1=Reserved
2-15=number of counters in each counter bank.

12.4

Non-Transparent Bridge

12.4.1

Definitions

Table 143: Link Definitions
Term
Description
NTB
Non-transparent bridge. A device that links the memory space of two separate systems together.
The processor implements a NTB that connects two systems together using the PCIe® interface.
12.4.2

Architecture

The processor contains a single PCIe® non-transparent bridge (NTB) device per node. A non-transparent bridge may be
used to link two systems together using a PCIe® interface. Conceptually, the NTB looks like a PCIe® device with two
endpoint interfaces and allows memory requests to cross between the two interfaces with translation logic used to keep the
two system address spaces separate.
From a functional standpoint, the NTB device itself is symmetric in nature but the connection paths to the endpoints are
asymmetric. The primary side of the NTB connects to one of the processor's internal root-complex ports. This side sends
DMA traffic to local system memory and receives MMIO and peer-to-peer traffic from the local system.
The secondary side of the NTB is tied to a physical PCIe® interface and connects to an external system. Port A of either
PCIe® controller on the same node may be programmed to change from a normal root-complex port to a switch upstream
port. The switch upstream port supports up to x16 width. Additional internal logic exposes a switch downstream port and
the secondary side NTB endpoint configuration space behind the externally facing switch upstream port.
12.4.2.1

NTB BAR Layout

Each side of the NTB appears as a PCIe® endpoint device. Each endpoint exposes 4 BARs. BAR0 contains control
registers. MSI-X interrupt controls are located inside BAR0. The MSI-X table starts at BAR0+8K while the MSI-X
pending bit array table starts at BAR0+12K.
BAR1 is a 32-bit BAR used to pass requests to the opposite side of the NTB. BAR23 and BAR45 are 64-bit BARs used
for the same purpose.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

969

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020
12.4.2.2

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

NTB BAR Sizing

The NTB supports the PCIe®-defined resizable BAR capability to configure the BAR size. BAR1 may be sized up to
4GB while BAR23 and BAR45 each support sizes up to 512GB. An initial BAR size may be set by SBIOS before PCI
enumeration using the procedure described below. An OS which supports resizable BAR may subsequently choose to
resize the BAR based on OS-specific criteria.
Each side of the NTB may be configured separately. The controls to expose the resizable BAR capability are located in
nBIF0 for the primary side NTB endpoint function and nBIF2 for the secondary side NTB endpoint function.

Once the resizable BAR capability is exposed, the BAR size may then be set using the following registers:
NBIFEPFNCFG::PCIE_BAR1_CNTL[BAR_SIZE]
NBIFEPFNCFG::PCIE_BAR2_CNTL[BAR_SIZE]
NBIFEPFNCFG::PCIE_BAR3_CNTL[BAR_SIZE]
Please refer to the register description in NBIFEPFNCFG::PCIE_BAR1_CNTL[BAR_SIZE] for the size encodings. The
programmed size must match a size indicated in the previously programmed RESIZE_SUPPORTED register for the
corresponding BAR.
12.4.2.3

NTB Initialization

The following table describes the programming instructions needed to configure the node to connect the NTB to one of
the PCIe® ports or to disconnect the NTB. Additional programming is needed to configure the PCIe® controller between
the root complex mode and the switch mode needed for NTB.
12.4.2.4

Back-to-Back Initialization

In some usage models, two identical systems may be connected together using the NTB either through a backplane
connection or a cable. The processor does not support data transfers when the PCIe® link is trained in a cross-link
configuration (ie. 2 downstream ports connected together or 2 upstream ports connected together). This can occur if both
systems expose a normal root port to the connecting link, or both systems expose a switch upstream port behind the NTB
to the connecting link.
Systems may use jumpers or switches to configure one of the systems to enable its NTB while the other system disables
its NTB and exposes a normal root port. If such indicators are not available, more complex dynamic negotiation is
possible to create a connection that avoids a cross-link condition. During link training, each system must check for a
possible cross-link condition. If one is detected, each side may randomly change the system between 2 possible NTB
configurations, and then retrain the link. This process must be repeated until the cross-link condition is eliminated.
The table below summarizes the 2 NTB configurations that the system may be configured as to resolve the cross-link
condition. In both cases, the internal path to primary side of the NTB is active, so both systems see a local NTB. Only
configuration B connects the secondary side of the NTB to a physical PCIe® interface. This creates 2 logical NTB paths
to connect the systems together but only one of the paths is active at any one time.

NTB Configuration B

PCIe® Port A is configured as a switch upstream port
NTB secondary side is disconnected from PCIe®
NTB secondary side is connected to PCIe® port A

12.4.2.4.1

Back-to-Back Hot-Add

The use of NTB configurations A and B is designed to facilitate hot-plug support for the PCIe® link connecting the 2
systems together. When in configuration A, PCIe® port A reports hot-add using the standard OS-visible PCIe® hot-plug
facilities. When in configuration B, MP1 firmware managing the link training process reports link-up to both the primary
and secondary side NTB drivers using the NTB to firmware mailbox.
After successful link training, the system in configuration A operates as if a new device has been connected to its root
port. This should look like a normal PCIe® root port hot-add. The OS on the configuration A system should load the NTB
driver for the external secondary side NTB. The system in configuration B does not see a PCIe® hot-add event because
the connected NTB was already connected on the primary side to its internal root port. It does not see a change in PCI
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

971

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

topology.
12.4.2.4.2

Back-to-Back Hot-Remove

In a hot-remove scenario, the MP1 firmware is responsible for placing the PCIe® interface into a low power state and
preparing for a future hot-add. The system in configuration A sees the external NTB connected to its root port undergo a
standard PCIe® hot-remove operation. The NTB driver running on this system is unloaded. The MP1 firmware running
on the system in configuration B signals link-down to the local NTB primary side driver.
12.4.2.4.3

Link-Up/Link-Down Signaling to Driver

Link-Up is signaled to the primary side driver via NTB::PINTSTA[PMISC0_INTSTA][0]. Similarly, link-down is
signaled to the primary side driver via NTB::PINTSTA[PMISC0_INTSTA][1]. These generate an interrupt to the primary
side driver if interrupts for the corresponding event are not masked.
Link-Up is signaled to the secondary side driver via NTB::SINTSTA[SMISC0_INTSTA][0]. Similarly, link-down is
signaled to the primary side driver via NTB::SINTSTA[SMISC0_INTSTA][1]. These generate an interrupt to the
secondary side driver if interrupts for the corresponding event are not masked.
The secondary side driver does not see link-down on a hot-remove event. The OS should signal the driver to unload when
the NTB is removed from the system.

Bits Description
31:16 Reserved.
15:8 SLUT_SIZEUNIT. Read-write. Reset: 00h. The translated granularity of the look-up-table translation window
on the secondary side. The granularity is a value of power-of-2 sizes starting from 4KB, it can be calculated by
4KB*(2^ SLUT_SIZEUNIT). 0 = 4KB; 1 = 8KB ; 2: 16KB; 3: 32KB; 4: 64KB ; 5: 128KB; .... Software should
take the responsibility to program a correct value.
7:2 Reserved.
1 SLUT_ALLOC. Read-write. Reset: 0.
Description: When the look-up-table resource on the secondary side is enable, this field allocates the entire lookup-table resource on the secondary side to one of the BARs (BAR1, BAR2/3, BAR4/5) on the secondary side, all
the other BARs on the secondary side use the direct address translations.
0 = It is allocated for SBAR2/3.
1 = It is allocated for SBAR4/5.
0 SLUT_EN. Read-write. Reset: 0.
Description: 1 = Enable the look-up-table resource on the secondary side. It can be used for one of the BARs
(BAR1, BAR2/3 and BAR4/5) on the secondary side.
0 = Disable the look-up-table resource on the secondary side.

12.5.2

Introduction

This document describes the PCI Express programming sequence for the PCIe® controller.
In order to support a wide variety of system topologies, the PCI Express (PCIe®) subsystem is highly configurable. The
PCIe® cores have been designed for, and incorporated into the PCIe® root complex fabric in a manner that ensures that
system BIOS has the opportunity and flexibility to configure the PCIe® capabilities to the required system topology.
Once the PCIe® subsystem has been configured to reflect the requirements and functionality of the system topology, the
individual PCIe® links are allowed to train and establish connections to PCIe® devices present in the system. Once the
links have been trained, system BIOS may pass control to the operating system or it may complete other tasks unrelated to
PCIe®.
12.5.3

12.5.3.1

Register Access

PCIe® IP Space

The upper-part of SMN address are known as Aperture ID used for routing the SMN packet to the correct IP. The remote
SMU (RSMU) inside the IP tile outputs a 20-bit lower-part SMN address for addressing registers of the IP. The upper 16
bits are also available on the Aperture ID port of the RSMU but are not expected to be used. This means that each
RSMU/IP is allocated a 1MB space. The SMN address decoder is responsible for decoding this 20-bit address. In PCIe®
IP, there are three register spaces available:
1. Per Port Configuration Space
• From the CPU's perspective, this is a direct access. The CPU issues the transaction through its normal data
path to IOHUB/nBIF. The IOHUB/nBIF detects that this is a configuration cycle and generates an SMN
transaction on the SMN network, constructing the 20-bit address.
• In the case where some other party needs to access the port's configuration space (for example the SMU)
it becomes the initiator of the SMN transaction, creating the 20-bit address and targets the correct IP with
the aperture ID (upper 16 bits).
2. Per Port Private Space
• From CPU's perspective, this is an indirect access. In each port's configuration space there is an aperture
defined by the PCIe® specification to access that ports private space. The CPU issues the transaction
through the normal data path to the IOHUB/nBIF. The IOHUB/nBIF is the entry point for the SMN and
generates the SMN packet to the correct IP with the correct 20-bit address.
• In the case where software needs to access the port's private space (for example the SMU), it becomes the
initiator of the SMN transaction, creating the 20-bit address, and targets the correct IP.
3. Per Core Private Space – Indirect Access
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

1011

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

•

It is not expected that third party software requires this space. Only the SBIOS and driver software are
expected to use the registers in this space.
• The software accesses this address space by using an aperture in:
1. Root Complex: the IOHUB's configuration space (Index/Data pair in nbconfig space).
2. Switch: nBIF's memory mapped space.
3. It is the responsibility of these two parties to intercept this transaction, decode it, and initiate the
SMN transaction. It needs to target the correct IP space and generate the correct 20 bit address.
• In the case where software needs to access the PCIe® core space (for example the SMU), it becomes the
initiator of the SMN transaction, creating the 20-bit address, and targets the correct IP.
From the system point of view, the PCIE IP space (20-Bit, 1MB) is shown below (in blue shaded area) and it can be
accessed by the 2 paths:

Figure 39: Allocated PCIe® space on the SMN
Bit[19] in the above figure allows the user to specify if the register access is a port register access or a core (PCIe® IP)
access.
Port Access:
Bit[18] only has meaning if bit[19] == 0 (port access) and specifies if the register access is targeting the ports
configuration space or the ports private space. Bits[17:12] provide the port number. This field allows software to access
different ports (ports start from 0). Bits[11:0] are the actual register addresses defined in the port's configuration or private
space.
Core (PCIe®) access:
If bit[19] == 1, then software is accessing the PCIe® registers. In this case, bit[18] is always 0. Bits[17:0] specify the
PCIe® IP space register address.

Pre-Link BIOS Initialization

1. After the SMU has handed over control to the SBIOS, the initialization process can commence. The first step the
SBIOS should take is to check if the reset process has been completed successfully. This can be done by checking
if the RESET_COMPLETE bit is set to 1 in the register SWRST_COMMAND_STATUS (example shown above).
2. The second step in the SBIOS initialization sequence must be to program the Straps using the RSMU Index/Data
pair method described above. This is where the topology settings, link configuration, selecting PCIe® Port 0's
mode (configure as Down Stream Port or Switch Upstream Port) and other aspects of the PCIe® IP can be
programmed.
3. To make the strap changes take effect inside the PCIe® IP, the reconfigure process must be used. The reconfigure
process puts the PCIe® Core logic into reset and then allows the updated Strap values to be propagated into the
PCIe® IP. Finally, the reconfigure process brings the PCIe® Core logic out of reset.
4. The final step for the SBIOS is to release hold training (Set register bits HOLD_TRAINING_<PORT> to 0) for
all the ports which need to function.

12.5.4.3.2

12.5.4.3.2.1

Port Re-ordering

Motivation for Additional Configurations and Routing Support

The evolution of PCI Express protocalhave enabled architectures that define a greater number of PCIe® links than were
supported on past products with the same number of dedicated PCIe® pins while maintaining or exceeding the
performance of existing products. This is accomplished by reducing the number of lanes per link but running the link at
higher data rates. In order to facilitate the change, without increasing the number of PCIe® cores that are deployed,
additional PCIe® configurations have been defined within this document. The implementation of of the PCIe® supports
up to 16 PCI Express lanes and up to 16 PCI Express links. In addition to the expanded configuration support, a more
flexible logical to physical lane routing strategy is implemented. Heretofore, the sole criterion used when the PCIe® IP
assigns its logical lanes to the physical lanes was the default link width. The link with the widest width was pegged to
physical lane 0. The link with the next widest width would be physical lane 1, and so on. This limited the flexibility of the
board level connections and it occasionally caused supplementary routing requirements at the SoC level or at the board
level. To alleviate the additional routing, PCIE4.0 allows the order in which logical lanes of each port are assigned to
physical lanes to be defined through port ordering registers (i.e., by software).
12.5.4.3.2.2

Port Re-Ordering Definition and Rules

The port re-ordering feature allows the end user to define the port order, through strap-loadable registers, at the same time
or after defining the configuration and prior to taking the IP out of reset.
One port level and one core level register is defined to identify the port to physical lane order for the PCIE block. The perport register is called "LC_PORT_ORDER" and the core register is called "LC_PORT_ORDER_CNTL". They are straploadable (STRAP_BIF_PORT_ORDER_<port>, STRAP_BIF_ PORT_ORDER_CNTL). The fields of the per-port
registers denote the offset (from lane 0) of the lanes on the given port. The core-level register controls the enabling and
disabling of the feature. By default, the feature is disabled and all offsets are set to 0x0. All the offsets must be
programmed when the feature is enabled upon initialization.
The "LC_PORT_ORDER" register fields and default settings are defined as follows:
• LC_PORT_OFFSET [3:0] R/W DEF=0x0
• RESERVED [31:4]
The "LC_PORT_ORDER_CNTL" register fields and default settings are defined as follows:
• LC_PORT_ORDER_EN [0] R/W DEF=0x0
• RESERVED [31:1]
The process of re-ordering the ports must follow the rules outlined in this section. Any violation of these rules results in
the PCIe® block reverting to the default port ordering (see section 5.1 of this document) and undefined behavior.
•
•

All settings of the LC_PORT_ORDER register field must be distinct (no duplicates are allowed). For example, if
LC_PORT_OFFSET for port A is set to 0x0, none of the other port fields must be set to 0x0. This leads to each
number in the range from 0x0 to 0xF (inclusive) being assigned at least once.
A later lettered port must not be placed ahead of an earlier lettered port of the same maximum link width. For
example, in a 16x16 instantiation, with the configuration set to ‘C', the potential orders for the 3 ports are: A, B, C
(x8/x4/x4); B, A, C (x4/x8/x4); and B, C, A (x4/x4/x8). A, C, B and C, B, A are not recognized as valid orders
because ‘C' is placed ahead of ‘B', although it has the same maximum link width.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

Lane Aggregation

This section depicts the physical pin to logical lane ID mapping as well as the possible ways in which the lanes may be
aggregated into links.
There are two PCIe® controllers in the design, with each in RC8x16 design configuration. Each PCIe® controller
supports as many as 8 ports and as many as 16 lanes. The ports combination can be 2:2:2:2:2:2:2:2, 1:1:2:2:2:2:2:4,
2:2:2:2:2:2:4, 4:4:4:4, 8:8, 16. Port reordering is supported to utilize the physical lanes which may be laid out differently
compared with the logical lane layout. And the logical lanes from PCIe® controller may not be fully connected with the
PHY lanes, which is limited from the maximum available physical lanes in the design. full size. PCIe® GFX has all its 16
lanes populated, while PCIe® GPP controller has its logical lane 5, 6, 7 and 8 tied off.
The supported lane configurations of PCIe® GFX controller are listed in Table 148 [PCIe® GFX lane configurations].
Physical lanes from 16 to 23 are also connected with SATA controller. Please refer to DXIO section of "Supported PHY
Sharing Configuration" for more information on sharing PHY lanes with multiple controllers.

Enabling Power-Saving Features

In order to reduce the average power-consumption of the PCIe® logic, the PCIe® controller and its core implement
several power-saving features. In order to ensure that the design emerges from reset in a safe manner, nearly all powersaving features are disabled by default. By disabling the power-saving features, there are fewer interactions to complicate
the boot process.
While some of the power-saving features have already been enabled by the preceding programming phases, many of the
power-saving features have not yet been enabled. This section breaks down the enablement of the power-saving features
into individual elements and provides the programming sequences, described as a set of steps and/or algorithms using
pseudo-code format with register mnemonics.

link reset event was caused by a link disable. Clearing the link reset request status bit (SWUS_LINK_RESET,
SWUS_LINK_RESET_CFG_ONLY, or SWUS_LINK_RESET_PHY_CALIB) clears this bit.
29 LINK_RESET_TYPE_HOT_RESET. Read-only. Reset: 0. 0=Not Detected. 1=Detected. Indicates if the link
reset event was caused by a hot reset. Clearing the link reset request status bit (SWUS_LINK_RESET,

28 SWDS_LINK_RESET_CFG_ONLY. Read-write. Reset: 0. 0=Not Detected. 1=Detected. (Switch Downstream

12.6

NBIF

12.6.1

Definitions

Table 150: Link Definitions
Term
Description
NBIF
New BIF
12.6.2

Introduction

The NBIO (North Bridge I/O) container is the sub-system design hierarchy that assembles the various NBIO blocks to
build a high performance and low power PCIe®-compatible I/O interconnect. The NBIO provides PCIe® connectivity to
external devices as well as AXI-based IPs.
The nBIF (new PCIe® Bus Interface) is one of the sub-IPs of the NBIO. The BIF is legacy AMD naming and normally
refers to the GPU card connection between the GFX/MM engine and the PCI fabric. The nBIF serves to build a PCIe®
system view and data path for both AMD specific clients and general 3rd-party IP clients.
•
•
•

Root Complex (RC) port (in APU mode) or switch downstream port (in discrete mode) PCIe® function
One multi-func PCIe® endpoint device
Stardard PCIe® features and AMD specific features

Generally, nBIF support 2 main directions of transactions:
• Host transactions, which come from upstream components and go to SMN or all kinds of GFX/Multimedia/3rdParty IPs.
• DMA transactions, which come from all kinds of GFX/Multimedia/3rd-Party IPs to upstream components.
This section describes the nBIF and the related features programming requirements.

[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Figure 42: nBIF System Hub Diagram
12.6.3

nBIF features

General nBIF System Hub features:
• SW.DS + EP configuration in single discrete mode
• Covers all AXI IPs connected through System Hub and performs SDP/AXI conversion for System Hub traffic
• Provides PCIe® software view for internal IPs including all System Hub clients
• PCIe® Advanced Error Reporting
12.6.4

Register Access

12.6.4.1

Access from SMN

All nBIF System Hub registers, including CFG registers or MMR or private registers, are mapped to SMN. All accesses
from SMN should use flattened 32-bit SMN addresses.
To leverage SMN security policy, even host register access from nBIF, nBIF would forward access to SMN, then receive
access from SMN. The access routing is performed by the SMN.
12.6.4.1.1

nBIF's SMN Aperture

Generally, nBIF's register in BIF's aperture consists of the following types:
• Per-function CFG registers for BIF.SWDS (or iRC) port functions and BIF.EP functions.
• VF configuration registers for certain PF with SRIOV support.
• MSI-X PBA and per-vector masking/pending bits.
• Some common register sets per endpoint function and per downstream port (32 32-bit DW per function at most).
The nBIF reserves one 4 KB to shadow PCIESWUS.CFG registers, which is re-allocated inside nBIF.
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

12.6.4.1.2

SystemHub SMN Aperture

The MMIO registers in SystemHub can be categorized into two groups:
• SystemHub/GDC private registers.
• GPV (Global Programmer View) in NIC-400.
[AMD Confidential - Distribution with NDA]

1182

AMD Confidential - Advance Information
56176 Rev 3.10 - Aug 18, 2020

PPR for AMD Family 17h Model 71h B0

Each ASIB/AMIB/IB inside NIC-400 is allocated with a 4 KB register block.
In SMN space, sixteen 1 MB apertures have assigned to SystemHub which sums up to 16 MB register space (AperID
0x14~0x23). Each SystemHub instance consumes a 2 MB space, so up-to 8 SystemHub instances can be accommodated.
The diagram below describes the register mapping methodology in 2 MB space and detailed mapping.
• The entire space is organized in unit of 4 KB page.
• The top 128 KB (16, 4 KB pages) is reserved for SystemHub/GDC private registers:
• The first 64 KB is for GDC MMReg.
• The next 60 KB is for SystemHub MMReg (Register for one SystemHub clock domain occupies 1, 4 KB).
• The last 4 KB is for GDC Non-MMIO Reg (The first 2 KB is for GDC_RST and the second 2 KB is for
GDC_RAS).
• The remaining spaces are reserved for NIC-400 switches.
• Each NIC-400 switch consumes consecutive 128 KB spaces (32, 4 KB pages), so a total of 15 NIC-400 switches
could be supported in one SystemHub instance.
• Inside 128 KB space for one NIC-400 switch:
• The first 16 (0~15) is assigned for ASIB.
• The next 8 (16~23) is assigned for AMIB.
• The next 7 (24~30) is assigned for IB.
• The last one (31) is assigned for GPV_master of this NIC-400 switch.

12.6.4.2

Configuration (CFG) Register Access from Host CPU

12.6.4.2.1

CFG Direct Access

All PCI Express configuration registers can be accessed directly by CFG type transactions.
nbif0 : RC-port0 + EP device0
nbif1 : RC-port0 + EP device0
RC-port1 + EP device1
RC-port2 + EP device2
nbif2 : SW.DS-port0 + EP device0
All configuration space registers are all mapped to 4 KB pages of nbif*cfg in SMN.
12.6.4.3

Direct Accessing nBIF Register for MMReg

The nBIF only owns some of the GFX MMRs. All other functions' MMR must be located in the client IPs.

For a Port with its Parity Error Response bit in the Command register set, indicates if either of the following two
conditions occurs on the primary interface:
1) Port receives a poisoned Completion going downstream
2) Port transmits a poisoned Request upstream.

item. This bit must be 1 for PCI Express.
3 INT_STATUS. Read-only. Reset: 0. 0=Not Detected. 1=Detected. Indicates if an INTx interrupt Message is
pending internally in the function.

Bits Description
31:0 BASE_ADDR. Read-only. Reset: Fixed,0000_0000h. Bit 0 is read-only and used to determine whether the
register maps into Memory or I/O space. Base Address registers that map into I/O Space are always 32bits wide
with bit 0 hardwired to 1b. Bit 1 is Reserved and must return 0b on reads and the other bits are used to map the
Function into I/O Space. Base Address registers that map into Memory Space can be 32 bits or 64 bits wide with
bit 0 hardwired to 0b. For Memory Base Address registers, bits 2 and 1 have an encoded meaning. 00 = Base
register is 32 bits wide and can be mapped anywhere in the 32 address bit Memory Space. 10 = Base register is 64
bits wide and can be mapped anywhere in the 64 address bit Memory Space. 01/11 = Reserved. For Memory Base
Address registers, Bit 3 indicate whether the data is prefetchable. For Memory Base Address registers, Bit 3 to Bit
0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 4 is RO-ZERO. For I/O Base Address registers, Bit 1 to Bit 0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 2 is ROZERO. N is determined by corresponding aperture size.

Bits Description
31:0 BASE_ADDR. Read-only. Reset: Fixed,0000_0000h. Bit 0 is read-only and used to determine whether the
register maps into Memory or I/O space. Base Address registers that map into I/O Space are always 32bits wide
with bit 0 hardwired to 1b. Bit 1 is Reserved and must return 0b on reads and the other bits are used to map the
Function into I/O Space. Base Address registers that map into Memory Space can be 32 bits or 64 bits wide with
bit 0 hardwired to 0b. For Memory Base Address registers, bits 2 and 1 have an encoded meaning. 00 = Base
register is 32 bits wide and can be mapped anywhere in the 32 address bit Memory Space. 10 = Base register is 64
bits wide and can be mapped anywhere in the 64 address bit Memory Space. 01/11 = Reserved. For Memory Base
Address registers, Bit 3 indicate whether the data is prefetchable. For Memory Base Address registers, Bit 3 to Bit
0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 4 is RO-ZERO. For I/O Base Address registers, Bit 1 to Bit 0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 2 is ROZERO. N is determined by corresponding aperture size.

Bits Description
31:0 BASE_ADDR. Read-only. Bit 0 is read-only and used to determine whether the register maps into Memory or
I/O space. Base Address registers that map into I/O Space are always 32bits wide with bit 0 hardwired to 1b. Bit 1
is Reserved and must return 0b on reads and the other bits are used to map the Function into I/O Space. Base
Address registers that map into Memory Space can be 32 bits or 64 bits wide with bit 0 hardwired to 0b. For
Memory Base Address registers, bits 2 and 1 have an encoded meaning. 00 = Base register is 32 bits wide and can
be mapped anywhere in the 32 address bit Memory Space. 10 = Base register is 64 bits wide and can be mapped
anywhere in the 64 address bit Memory Space. 01/11 = Reserved. For Memory Base Address registers, Bit 3
indicate whether the data is prefetchable. For Memory Base Address registers, Bit 3 to Bit 0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 4
is RO-ZERO. For I/O Base Address registers, Bit 1 to Bit 0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 2 is RO-ZERO. N is determined
by corresponding aperture size.

31:0 BASE_ADDR. Bit 0 is read-only and used to determine whether the register maps into Memory or I/O space.
Base Address registers that map into I/O Space are always 32bits wide with bit 0 hardwired to 1b. Bit 1 is
Reserved and must return 0b on reads and the other bits are used to map the Function into I/O Space. Base
Address registers that map into Memory Space can be 32 bits or 64 bits wide with bit 0 hardwired to 0b. For
Memory Base Address registers, bits 2 and 1 have an encoded meaning. 00 = Base register is 32 bits wide and can
be mapped anywhere in the 32 address bit Memory Space. 10 = Base register is 64 bits wide and can be mapped
anywhere in the 64 address bit Memory Space. 01/11 = Reserved. For Memory Base Address registers, Bit 3
indicate whether the data is prefetchable. For Memory Base Address registers, Bit 3 to Bit 0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 4
is RO-ZERO. For I/O Base Address registers, Bit 1 to Bit 0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 2 is RO-ZERO. N is determined
by corresponding aperture size.

Bits Description
31:0 BASE_ADDR. Read-write. Reset: 0000_0000h. Bit 0 is read-only and used to determine whether the register
maps into Memory or I/O space. Base Address registers that map into I/O Space are always 32bits wide with bit 0
hardwired to 1b. Bit 1 is Reserved and must return 0b on reads and the other bits are used to map the Function
into I/O Space. Base Address registers that map into Memory Space can be 32 bits or 64 bits wide with bit 0
hardwired to 0b. For Memory Base Address registers, bits 2 and 1 have an encoded meaning. 00 = Base register is
32 bits wide and can be mapped anywhere in the 32 address bit Memory Space. 10 = Base register is 64 bits wide
and can be mapped anywhere in the 64 address bit Memory Space. 01/11 = Reserved. For Memory Base Address
registers, Bit 3 indicate whether the data is prefetchable. For Memory Base Address registers, Bit 3 to Bit 0 is RO,
Bit N to Bit 4 is RO-ZERO. For I/O Base Address registers, Bit 1 to Bit 0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 2 is RO-ZERO. N is
determined by corresponding aperture size.

31:0 BASE_ADDR. Read-write. Reset: 0000_0000h. Bit 0 is read-only and used to determine whether the register
maps into Memory or I/O space. Base Address registers that map into I/O Space are always 32bits wide with bit 0
hardwired to 1b. Bit 1 is Reserved and must return 0b on reads and the other bits are used to map the Function
into I/O Space. Base Address registers that map into Memory Space can be 32 bits or 64 bits wide with bit 0
hardwired to 0b. For Memory Base Address registers, bits 2 and 1 have an encoded meaning. 00 = Base register is
32 bits wide and can be mapped anywhere in the 32 address bit Memory Space. 10 = Base register is 64 bits wide
and can be mapped anywhere in the 64 address bit Memory Space. 01/11 = Reserved. For Memory Base Address
registers, Bit 3 indicate whether the data is prefetchable. For Memory Base Address registers, Bit 3 to Bit 0 is RO,
Bit N to Bit 4 is RO-ZERO. For I/O Base Address registers, Bit 1 to Bit 0 is RO, Bit N to Bit 2 is RO-ZERO. N is
determined by corresponding aperture size.
